Priam considers and rejects Achilles’ proposal to marry Polyxena.
Aesacus is Priam's son by Arisbe.
Laodamia, daughter of Bellerophon, is Sarpedon's mother.
Sarpedon and Rhadamanthus are sons of Zeus and Europa.

relations.myth: Recovery and burial of the fallen Seven
relations.note: Theseus defeats the Thebans and recovers the fallen attackers’ bodies for burial.

relations.myth: Peaceful recovery of the fallen Seven
relations.note: A competing tradition says Theseus recovered their bodies through agreement rather than conquest.
Sisyphus is placed near Tantalus among exemplary underworld sufferers.

god_relations.note: Thetis is Achilles’ divine mother.

god_relations.myth: Removal from the funeral pyre to Leuke
god_relations.note: Thetis snatches Achilles from his pyre and conveys him to Leuke.
Achilles is Zeus’ great-grandson through Aegina and Aeacus.

god_relations.myth: Thetis secures honor through Achaean losses
god_relations.note: Zeus grants Thetis’ request to honor Achilles by permitting Greek defeats.
Hera supports Achilles’ Achaean side and sends Hephaestus against Scamander.
Athena restrains Achilles before he can kill Agamemnon.
Athena supports Achilles and deceives Hector during their fatal encounter.
Apollo repeatedly opposes Achilles, striking Patroclus and preserving Hector’s corpse.
Apollo helps Paris kill Achilles; some Classical accounts make Apollo effectively the killer.
Hephaestus makes Achilles’ replacement armor and cosmic shield at Thetis’ request.
Hephaestus checks the attacking river with divine fire.
Poseidon intervenes against Achilles’ attack by carrying Aeneas away.
Later tradition says Poseidon creates or grants Leuke for Achilles.
Aphrodite frustrates Achilles’ abuse by preserving Hector’s corpse from damage.
Hermes guides Priam safely into and out of Achilles’ camp.
Chiron teaches Achilles hunting, medicine, music, and heroic discipline.
The Nereids join Thetis in lamenting Achilles for seventeen days.
The Muses lament Achilles during his prolonged funeral observances.
Actaeon accompanies Artemis in hunting before unwillingly seeing her bath.
Artemis gives Actaeon deer-form so his dogs kill him.
Actaeon claims superiority in hunting and incurs Artemis' deadly punishment.
Diana transforms Actaeon into a stag after he unknowingly enters her grotto.
Artemis punishes Actaeon's erotic spying by transforming him for his hounds.
Zeus becomes angry because Actaeon woos Semele, causing Actaeon's death.
Chiron rears or trains Actaeon in hunting.
Chiron creates an image of Actaeon that consoles the grieving dogs.
Actaeon is Harmonia's maternal grandson through Autonoe.
Harmonia mourns Actaeon after his destruction.
Actaeon descends from Ares through Harmonia and Autonoe.
Actaeon descends from Aphrodite through Harmonia and Autonoe.
Actaeon is Apollo's grandson through Aristaeus in the standard paternal genealogy.
Actaeon's ghost laments that his divine grandfather Apollo did not save him.
Actaeon and Dionysus are first cousins through the sisters Autonoe and Semele.
Actaeon's dismemberment foreshadows Dionysus' destruction of their cousin Pentheus.
Athena recounts Actaeon's fate as precedent when explaining Tiresias' lesser punishment.

god_relations.myth: Oracle of the lion and boar
god_relations.note: Apollo gives the oracle governing the marriages of Adrastus's daughters.
Apollo's response commands Adrastus and Hipponous to cast themselves into fire.

god_relations.myth: Settlement after recovery of the Argive dead
god_relations.note: Athena orders an Argive oath binding Adrastus after Theseus recovers the bodies.
Cleisthenes transfers Adrastus's tragic choruses to Dionysus.

god_relations.myth: Gift of the divine horse Arion
god_relations.note: Heracles gives Arion to Adrastus; no personal encounter appears in earlier evidence.

god_relations.myth: Learned derivation of the title Adrasteia
god_relations.note: Late writers associate Adrasteia's title with Adrastus, without proving original identity.
A Pausanian tradition credits Adrastus with founding a sanctuary of Nemesis.
Zeus sends unfavorable signs, but Adrastus proceeds with the expedition.

god_relations.myth: Destruction of Adrastus's champions at Thebes
god_relations.note: Zeus kills Capaneus and opens the earth to preserve Amphiaraus from dishonor.
Apollo sends plague because Agamemnon dishonors Chryses and retains Chryseis.
Artemis blocks the fleet and demands Iphigenia after Agamemnon kills her deer and boasts.
Artemis frustrates the intended sacrifice by substituting a deer and taking Iphigenia.
Athena prevents Achilles from killing Agamemnon during their quarrel.
Athena supports the Achaeans fighting under Agamemnon's command.
Zeus sends Agamemnon a false dream promising immediate victory.
Zeus permits Achaean losses against Agamemnon's coalition to vindicate Achilles.
Agamemnon's inherited sceptre originates with Zeus before passing through the Pelopid dynasty.
Hera supports the Achaean army under Agamemnon's leadership.
Hephaestus makes the divine sceptre that Agamemnon eventually inherits.
Hermes passes the future sceptre of Agamemnon from Zeus to Pelops.
Thetis secures Zeus' action against Agamemnon's army for dishonoring Achilles.
Ajax is Zeus’s great-grandson through Aeacus and Telamon.
Zeus answers Heracles’ prayer by sending an eagle omen.
Zeus grants Ajax light in which to continue fighting.
Athena contrives Odysseus’s victory over Ajax in the armor contest.
Athena deludes Ajax into attacking livestock instead of Greek commanders.
Poseidon, disguised as Calchas, encourages Ajax and renews his strength.
Apollo restores Hector after Ajax knocks him down with a stone.
Apollo helps Paris kill Achilles before Ajax recovers the corpse.
Heracles prays for Ajax’s birth and interprets Zeus’s eagle omen.
Heracles wraps the infant in lion skin, leaving one vulnerable spot.
Thetis, Peleus’s wife and Achilles’s mother, is Ajax’s aunt by marriage.
Thetis sets Achilles’s armor out as the prize disputed by Ajax.
Ajax invokes Hermes Chthonios for a swift and painless death.
Ajax invokes the Erinyes to punish the Atreidae and Greek army.
Apollo serves Admetus as a herdsman after Zeus punishes him.
Apollo protects Admetus because the king treated him piously during servitude.
Apollo yokes a lion and boar, enabling Admetus to win Alcestis.
Artemis fills Admetus’ bridal chamber with snakes after he omits her sacrifice.
Thanatos claims Alcestis when she substitutes herself for Admetus.
Alcestis is received, or is about to be received, among underworld powers.
An alternative tradition has Persephone send Alcestis back without Heracles.
Admetus conceals Alcestis’ death and hospitably receives Heracles at Pherae.
Heracles overpowers Thanatos and returns the veiled Alcestis to Admetus.
Plutarch says Heracles’ love for Admetus motivates Alcestis’ recovery.
Castor and Admetus are co-members of later heroic expedition lists.

god_relations.myth: Zeus impersonates Amphitryon and lies with Alcmene
god_relations.note: Zeus deceives Alcmene by assuming Amphitryon’s appearance and fathers Heracles.

god_relations.myth: Zeus impersonates Amphitryon during the extended night
god_relations.note: Zeus usurps Amphitryon’s identity, reports his victory, and sleeps with Alcmene.
Zeus apparently vindicates Alcmene by sending rain against Amphitryon’s attempted burning.

god_relations.myth: Zeus orders Alcmene removed to the Blessed Isles
god_relations.note: Later tradition makes Zeus command Alcmene’s bodily removal and substitution with a stone.
Hera restrains Alcmene’s delivery so Eurystheus is born first and gains sovereignty.

god_relations.myth: Hera sends serpents against the infant twins
god_relations.note: Hera attacks Alcmene’s household by sending two serpents against Heracles and Iphicles.
The birth-goddess prevents Alcmene from delivering until deceived by a female helper.
Hecate transforms Galinthias and later makes Alcmene’s helper her sacred attendant.
Mercury impersonates Sosia and helps Jupiter maintain the deception of Alcmene and Amphitryon.

god_relations.myth: Hermes carries Alcmene to the Blessed Isles
god_relations.note: At Zeus’s command, Hermes substitutes a stone and transports Alcmene to the Blessed Isles.

god_relations.myth: Helios delays sunrise during Zeus’s extended night
god_relations.note: Zeus orders Helios not to rise while Alcmene is deceived by the divine impersonation.

god_relations.myth: Selene cooperates in extending Alcmene’s night
god_relations.note: Some later accounts enlist Selene in the cosmic pause enabling Zeus’s deception.
Personified Night is associated with the prolonged night surrounding Alcmene’s conception of Heracles.

god_relations.myth: Poseidon’s golden hair protects Amphitryon’s enemy
god_relations.note: Poseidon gives Pterelaus the life-preserving hair that structures Amphitryon’s Taphian war.

god_relations.myth: Athena stops mad Heracles from killing Amphitryon
god_relations.note: Athena strikes Heracles unconscious with a stone, saving Amphitryon from his murderous madness.
Apollo’s oracle resolves the Heracleidae’s dispute by directing that Alcmene be buried at Megara.
Alcmene is Heracles’ biological mother by Zeus.
Amphitryon is Heracles’ social and putative father, expressed by the Homeric patronymic.
Amphitryon acts as Heracles’ benevolent instructor and teaches him to drive a chariot.

god_relations.myth: Amphitryon fights beside Heracles against the Minyans
god_relations.note: Amphitryon joins Heracles in battle against the Minyans of Orchomenus.

god_relations.myth: Heracles returns and saves Amphitryon’s household
god_relations.note: Heracles returns before Lycus can execute Amphitryon, Megara, and the children.
Hera-driven madness turns Heracles against his household, leaving Amphitryon in mortal danger.

god_relations.myth: Hebe and Alcmene share the Cynosarges cult group
god_relations.note: Hebe receives cult alongside Alcmene, Heracles, and Iolaus without a surviving direct narrative.
Zeus loves and favors Amphiaraus.
Zeus splits the earth before Periclymenus can strike Amphiaraus.
Apollo loves Amphiaraus and provides his prophetic affiliation.
A late genealogy names Apollo as Amphiaraus’ father.
Harmonia’s necklace passes through Polynices to Eriphyle and determines Amphiaraus’ departure.
Amphiaraus frustrates Athena’s plan to immortalize the wounded Tydeus.
Castor hunts beside Amphiaraus and neighbors him on the Tegea pediment.
Amphiaraus adopts Asclepian healing methods and bearded physician iconography without identification.
Hermes shares a division of the great Oropian altar with Amphiaraus.
Hestia shares a division of the great Oropian altar with Amphiaraus.
Heracles receives worship on another division of Amphiaraus’ great Oropian altar.
Aphrodite receives worship on another division of Amphiaraus’ Oropian altar.
Pan receives worship on another division of Amphiaraus’ Oropian altar.
The nymphs receive worship on Amphiaraus’ divided altar at Oropos.
Aphrodite gave Andromache the marriage veil that falls during her collapse.
Artemis kills Andromache’s ransomed mother in Priam’s house.
Andromache seeks divine protection from Hermione’s plot at Thetis’ altar.
Thetis guarantees her marriage to Helenus and the continuation of Molossus’ dynasty.
Offended by Cassiopeia’s comparison, they seek the punishment that places Andromeda in danger.
Poseidon sends flood and monster, indirectly making Andromeda the demanded victim.
Medusa’s severed head is used by Perseus against Phineus and his followers.
Athena places or helps place Andromeda’s image among the stars.
Zeus is Andromeda’s divine father-in-law through Perseus.

Andromeda is an ancestress of Heracles through Electryon and Alcmena.
Their separate rescue scenes are juxtaposed as parallel Argive victories.

Antigone is poetically presented as a bride proceeding to Hades.
The chorus compares Antigone's enclosure with Danaë's imprisonment.
They are invoked as supernatural agents of Antigone's family's ruin.
Athena raises Arachne and teaches her the art of weaving.
Athena transforms Arachne and Phalanx into crawling creatures after their incest.
Virgil alludes to a spider hated by Minerva without naming Arachne.
Aelian contrasts spiders with Athena's weaving gift in a probable Arachne allusion.
Athena transforms Arachne using Hecatean herbs; Hecate does not personally act.

god_relations.myth: Construction and passage through the rocks
god_relations.note: Athena directs Argo’s construction and pushes the ship through the clashing rocks.
Hera protects Argo, favors Jason and engineers Medea’s aid and the return.
Apollo provides light that saves the company from supernatural darkness near Anaphe.
The company sacrifices to Apollo and witnesses his appearance above the sea at Thynias.
Zeus indirectly adjudicates the company’s blood pollution and sends ominous storm signs.
Aphrodite deploys Eros so Medea will assist Jason and the expedition.
Hecate supplies the ritual power Medea invokes to protect Jason during his trials.
The company steals the Fleece guarded within Ares’ Colchian grove and precinct.
The company confronts the fire-breathing bronze bulls made by Hephaestus for Aeëtes.
Thetis leads the Nereids in guiding and carrying Argo through western dangers.
The Nereids pass Argo hand to hand safely through the Planctae.
Triton guides Argo out of Lake Tritonis and receives the company’s tripod.
The company, through Euphemus, gives Triton a tripod after receiving his guidance.
Heracles joins under Jason, saves the party at Cyzicus and is left searching for Hylas.
Polyphemus searches for Hylas and is left behind when Argo departs Mysia.
Castor sails as the company’s horseman and combatant.
The Boreads pursue the Harpies and force an end to their attacks on Phineus.
Iris stops the Boreads from killing the Harpies and guarantees their oath.
After Talos blocks the landing, Medea and the company bring about his death.
Circe purifies Jason and Medea of blood guilt, then dismisses the company.
The Sirens try to lure the company, but Orpheus overpowers their song.
Scylla threatens Argo, but divine guidance enables the company to avoid her.
Charybdis threatens Argo, but divine guidance enables the company to avoid her.
She supplies Atalanta’s rival with golden apples used to defeat her.

Venus incites Atalanta and Hippomenes to sacrilegious desire after his ingratitude.
Atalanta hunts the monstrous boar sent by Artemis against Calydon.
Some late explanations make Artemis transform Atalanta after her broken virginity.
Zeus transforms Atalanta and Melanion into lions after sanctuary intercourse.
She transforms Atalanta and Hippomenes into lions and yokes them.
Hyginus makes Ares father Parthenopaeus by Atalanta without narrating their encounter.
Castor is a named fellow hunter alongside Atalanta.
Polydeuces is a named fellow hunter alongside Atalanta.
Homer names Glaucus as Bellerophon’s mortal father.

Poseidon fathers Bellerophon on Eurynome in Glaucus’ household.
Bellerophon sacrifices to Poseidon after receiving Athena’s golden bridle.
Athena appears in a dream and gives Bellerophon the golden bridle.
Pegasus carries Bellerophon while they kill the Chimera.
Pegasus bears Bellerophon against the Chimera, Amazons, and Solymi.
Pegasus throws Bellerophon to earth during his attempted heavenly ascent.
Bellerophon kills the fire-breathing, composite monster in Lycia.
Bellerophon is the grandfather of Glaucus through Hippolochus.
Bellerophon seeks the heavenly dwellings and the company of Zeus.
Europa is Cadmus’s sister or close kinswoman in Agenorid traditions.
Her abduction by Zeus launches Cadmus’s unsuccessful wandering and search.
Apollo directs Cadmus to abandon the search, follow a cow, and found a city.
Apollo attends and plays at the wedding in expanded accounts.
Cadmus sacrifices the guiding cow to Athena at the foundation site.
Athena instructs Cadmus to sow the slain dragon’s teeth.
Athena grants or validates Cadmus’s rule after his service to Ares.

Ares ultimately rescues Cadmus and Harmonia to the land of the blessed.
Hyginus makes Cadmus’s transformation punishment for killing Ares’s dragon.
Harmonia is Cadmus’s wife and the mother of his principal children.
Cadmus and Harmonia marry at a feast attended by the gods.
The spouses lead the Encheleans, defeat Illyrians, and rule together.
Cadmus and Harmonia are jointly transformed into serpents.
Zeus gives Harmonia to Cadmus as his bride in one account.
Zeus sends the transformed Cadmus and Harmonia to Elysium.

Aphrodite is a wedding participant or gift-giver in later accounts.
Hephaestus makes or gives Harmonia’s necklace in one tradition.
The Muses sing at Cadmus’s divine wedding.

Cadmus is Dionysus’s maternal grandfather through Semele.
Cadmus dresses as a Bacchant, dances, and accepts his grandson’s cult.
Dionysus prophesies Cadmus’s serpent form, warfare, and eventual rescue.
Thetis’s wedding to Peleus is poetically compared with Cadmus’s wedding.
Disguised as a shepherd, Cadmus distracts Typhon with music for Zeus.
Cadmus assists Zeus’s campaign against Typhon through musical deception.

god_relations.myth: Zeus assaults Callisto while disguised as Artemis
god_relations.note: Zeus assumes Artemis’ or Apollo’s form and rapes or impregnates Callisto.

god_relations.myth: Zeus conceals Callisto by transforming her
god_relations.note: One variant makes Zeus transform Callisto into a bear to conceal her.
Zeus saves Callisto from death or further danger by placing her among the stars.
Callisto hunts with Artemis, imitates her clothing, and vows to remain a virgin.
Artemis discovers the pregnancy and expels Callisto from her company.

god_relations.note: Hesiodic and Amphis-derived variants make Artemis transform Callisto as punishment.
Artemis kills bear-shaped Callisto, either through Hera’s prompting or broken-vow anger.

god_relations.myth: Hera transforms Callisto after Arcas’ birth
god_relations.note: Jealous Hera transforms Callisto into a bear after she bears Arcas.

god_relations.myth: Hera induces Artemis to shoot Callisto
god_relations.note: In one variant Hera persuades Artemis to kill the bear-shaped Callisto.
At Juno’s request, Tethys prevents catasterized Callisto from entering the sea.
Juno petitions Oceanus to prevent Callisto and Arcas from setting into his waters.
Apollo desires Cassandra and seeks sexual possession after promising prophetic power.
After receiving prophecy, Cassandra breaks her promise or faith with Apollo.
Apollo teaches Cassandra prophecy in expectation of sexual access.
Apollo makes Cassandra’s truthful prophecies unable to persuade after her refusal.
Apollo’s spit imposes the disabling condition that Cassandra will not be believed.
Cassandra clings to Athena’s image, from which Ajax violently drags her.
Cassandra perceives the avenging powers haunting the House of Atreus.
Cassandra prays to the Sun before entering the palace to die.
Castor is Clytemnestra’s brother and, in Hyginus, shares Tyndareus as father.
Castor marched against Agamemnon after Clytemnestra’s coerced marriage.
Pollux is Clytemnestra’s half-brother under Hyginus’ divided-paternity genealogy.
With Castor, Polydeuces threatened Agamemnon after Clytemnestra’s forced marriage.

Aphrodite afflicts Clytemnestra and her sisters with marital infidelity.
Clytemnestra opposes Artemis’ demand for Iphigenia’s sacrifice.
Apollo’s oracle authorizes the matricide that brings about Clytemnestra’s death.
Her ghost condemns Apollo for protecting Orestes while neglecting her blood claim.
Athena adjudicates the matricide in which Clytemnestra is the absent dead victim.

Clytemnestra’s ghost rouses them and commissions their pursuit of Orestes.
Clytemnestra prays to Zeus Teleios while preparing her design against Agamemnon.
Daedalus constructs a dancing place for Ariadne at Knossos.
Daedalus advises Ariadne to give Theseus the guiding thread.
Daedalus's artificial cow enables Pasiphae to conceive the Minotaur.
Daedalus builds the labyrinth that conceals and confines the Minotaur.
Daedalus constructs the cow-shaped apparatus enabling Pasiphae's union with the bull.
Pasiphae supplies Daedalus with a ship or conceals him from Minos.
Poseidon's punishment creates the crisis for which Daedalus constructs Pasiphae's cow.
Daedalus kills his inventive pupil and nephew out of jealousy.
Daedalus dedicates a wooden image of Heracles in thanks for an unspecified benefit.
Heracles recognizes and buries Daedalus's drowned son in the sail variant.
Daedalus dedicates his wings to Apollo after reaching Cumae.
Daedalus makes Apollo's temple doors depicting the Cretan story.
Daedalus constructs a sanctuary support and golden ram for Aphrodite.
A comic wooden Hermes claims Daedalus made him able to speak and walk.
Homer compares Hephaestus's divine craftsmanship with Daedalus's human work at Knossos.
A variant genealogy names Dionysus rather than Oeneus as her father.
Dionysus intervenes so Deianira and Gorge are spared or restored.
Heracles wins Deianira’s hand and becomes her husband.
Heracles shoots Nessus while the centaur assaults or abducts Deianira.
Deianira unwittingly sends the garment whose poison causes Heracles’ mortal death.
Hyginus says Heracles seduced or impregnated an alternate Deianira after promising marriage.
In the confused variant, Heracles rescues the woman called Deianira from Eurytion.
Aphrodite poetically presides as umpire over the bridal struggle.
Deianira’s garment takes effect while Heracles sacrifices to his father Zeus.
Deianira contrasts Hera’s glorious persecution of Hercules with Venus’ humiliating power.
Artemis transforms Meleager’s mourning sisters; Deianira is spared or subsequently restored.
Hebe becomes Heracles’ divine wife after Deianira has died.
Athena appears beside Deianira in some vase scenes of the Achelous contest.
Hermes appears beside Deianira in some vase scenes of the Achelous contest.
Deucalion is repeatedly named as Prometheus's son.

god_relations.myth: Prometheus warns Deucalion before the flood
god_relations.note: Prometheus warns Deucalion and directs him to provision and build a chest.
Pyrrha is the daughter of Epimetheus in the canonical genealogy.

god_relations.myth: Parnassian descent and settlement at Opus
god_relations.note: The couple descends from Parnassus and settles by Zeus's ordinance.
Zeus sends the flood against the Bronze race; the couple survives.
After Deucalion sacrifices, Zeus offers him a wish through Hermes.
Deucalion sacrifices to Zeus Phyxios after leaving the chest.
Zeus orders the stone procedure that allows the couple to restore humanity.

god_relations.myth: Jupiter commands the throwing of stones
god_relations.note: Jupiter directly commands Deucalion and Pyrrha to throw stones.
Jupiter destroys humanity but preserves the righteous and pious couple.
Hermes communicates Zeus's offered wish, prompting Deucalion to request people.

god_relations.myth: Oracle of the Great Mother's bones
god_relations.note: Themis instructs the couple cryptically to cast their mother's bones behind them.
Deucalion identifies Earth's stones as the Great Mother's bones in Themis's oracle.
Neptune summons rivers and strikes the earth, indirectly threatening the couple.
Triton blows his conch to recall the waters after Jupiter ends the flood.
The Syrian Deucalion builds a temple and altars in Atargatis's sanctuary landscape.
Athena grants Diomedes strength, radiance, divine sight, and permission to wound Aphrodite.
Athena heals Diomedes after Pandarus wounds him.
Athena conceals herself, deflects Ares’ spear, and drives Diomedes’ attack.
Athena sends an omen and guides Diomedes and Odysseus during their raid.
Athena guides Diomedes safely home from Troy in the Homeric return.
Athena makes Diomedes an immortal god.
Diomedes wounds Aphrodite’s hand while she carries Aeneas from battle.
Aphrodite avenges her wound by corrupting Aegialeia against Diomedes.
Aphrodite punishes Diomedes indirectly by transforming his companions into birds.
Diomedes wounds Ares with Athena’s concealment, protection, and decisive assistance.
Diomedes advances three times against Apollo before the god repels and warns him.
Aphrodite and Ares complain to Zeus after Diomedes wounds them.
Zeus removes Glaucus’ judgment during his unequal exchange with Diomedes.
Hera supports the Achaean side during Diomedes’ greatest battlefield successes.
Hephaestus saves Idaeus after Diomedes kills Idaeus’ brother Phegeus.
Diomedes and Glaucus refuse combat after recognizing inherited guest-friendship.
Diomedes exchanges bronze armor for Glaucus’ far more valuable gold armor.
Electra joins invocations asking underworld Hermes to guide or support the avengers.
Electra prays to Persephone for victory while performing rites at Agamemnon’s tomb.
Electra and Orestes ask Earth to send up or empower their father’s spirit.

Castor includes Polydeuces when speaking of the Dioscuri, without a separate exchange.

Electra invokes Ares chiefly as a divine image of murderous violence.

Hecuba accuses Helen of disguising personal desire as Aphrodite's compulsion.

Hecuba selects Athena's robe and convenes the women, but Athena refuses their prayer.
Lycophron makes transformed Hecuba a terrifying canine attendant of Hecate.

Nemesis bears Helen after Zeus pursues and impregnates her.

Aphrodite leads Helen astray from husband, child, and parents.

Hera creates Helen’s cloud-image while the real Helen is taken to Egypt.

Apollo makes Helen immortal and orders her worship as sailors’ protector.
Zeus is Heracles’ biological father through union with Alcmene.
Zeus rescues Heracles from the storm sent by Hera.
Zeus admits Heracles to Olympus after his mortal death.
Hera delays Heracles’ birth and secures Eurystheus’ precedence.
Hera sends two snakes, which the infant Heracles strangles.
Hera causes or commands the madness in which Heracles kills his family.
Heracles wounds Hera during their prolonged divine hostility.
Heracles and Hera are reconciled when he joins the Olympians.
Athena repeatedly protects and assists Heracles during his exploits.
Athena gives Heracles bronze rattles for driving out the birds.
Athena strikes Heracles unconscious, preventing him from killing Amphitryon.
Apollo’s Delphic oracle directs Heracles toward purification and Eurystheus’ service.
Heracles fights Apollo after seizing the tripod when refused an oracle.
Apollo confronts Heracles over the capture of Artemis’ sacred hind.
Artemis confronts Heracles for capturing her sacred hind.
Hermes assists, conducts or equips Heracles in labour and Underworld traditions.
Poseidon opposes Heracles during the Pylian campaign.
Hades permits Heracles to take Cerberus if he uses no weapons.
Heracles wounds Hades during an otherwise incompletely preserved conflict.
Persephone receives Heracles and intervenes in Underworld traditions.
Ares fights Heracles while defending his son Cycnus.
Hephaestus makes the bronze clappers Athena provides to Heracles.
Heracles threatens Helios with his bow during the western journey.
Helios lends Heracles his golden cup for crossing Ocean.
Heracles wrestles and restrains Nereus to obtain directions.
Heracles wrestles Triton in prominent Archaic visual representations.
Heracles wrestles and defeats Death to restore Alcestis.
Iris commands Lyssa to inflict madness upon Heracles for Hera.
Heracles marries the divine personification of youth on Olympus.
Nike appears with Heracles in cultic and victorious imagery.
Themis participates in divine knowledge concerning Heracles’ apotheosis.
At Hera’s order, Eileithyia delays Alcmene’s delivery of Heracles.
Dionysus and Heracles fight together in Gigantomachy traditions.
Heracles frees Prometheus by killing the eagle that torments him.
Prometheus directs Heracles toward Atlas and the Hesperides.
Heracles holds the sky while Atlas retrieves the apples.
Heracles tricks Atlas into resuming the burden of the sky.
Pan occasionally appears beside Heracles in regional cult and art.
Greek interpretation identifies the Tyrian god Melqart as Heracles.
Heracles strangles or clubs the invulnerable lion and takes its hide.
Heracles destroys the many-headed Hydra and poisons his arrows with its bile.
Heracles drives the boar through snow and captures it alive.
Heracles frightens the birds into flight and shoots them.
Heracles kills Geryon’s two-headed guard dog.
Heracles kills the triple-bodied cattle owner and takes his herd.
In one version Heracles kills Ladon and takes the golden apples.
Heracles subdues Cerberus unarmed, displays him, then returns him to Hades.
Heracles accidentally wounds Chiron with a Hydra-poisoned arrow.
Polyphemus joins Heracles in searching Mysia for the abducted Hylas.
Poseidon’s bull terrifies the horses, causing Hippolytus’ fatal chariot wreck.
She punishes his refusal of her honors by making Phaedra desire him.
He hunts in Artemis’ company, praises her chastity and offers her a garland.
Artemis reveals his innocence, reconciles him with Theseus and promises lasting cult.
Troezenian tradition credited Hippolytus with founding Artemis Lykeia’s local temple.
The divine healer reassembles or revives Hippolytus after his fatal chariot wreck.
An Epidaurian stele reportedly recorded his dedication of twenty horses to Asclepius.
Diana entrusts the resurrected Hippolytus, now Virbius, to Egeria’s grove.
Hippolytus recounts his suffering to console Egeria after Numa’s death.

god_relations.myth: Zeus pursues and sexually coerces Io
god_relations.note: Zeus desires Io; accounts describe seduction, coercion, or rape.
Zeus is Io’s divine partner and father of Epaphus.

god_relations.myth: Io is changed into a heifer
god_relations.note: Zeus transforms Io into a cow to conceal their encounter.

god_relations.myth: Io regains human form in Egypt
god_relations.note: Zeus secures or performs Io’s restoration after her wanderings.
Io serves as Hera’s priestess or cult-attendant at Argos.

god_relations.myth: Hera claims Io and sends the gadfly
god_relations.note: Hera confines Io under Argus and drives her wandering with a gadfly.
Some later summaries make Hera, rather than Zeus, transform Io.

god_relations.myth: Hermes kills Argus and releases Io
god_relations.note: Zeus sends Hermes to free Io by killing her vigilant guard.
Argus confines and watches Io until Hermes kills him.

god_relations.myth: Prometheus foretells Io’s route and descendants
god_relations.note: The bound Titan explains Io’s suffering and reveals her future wanderings and lineage.
Heracles is Io’s remote descendant, prophesied to free Prometheus.
Apollo indirectly commands Inachus to expel Io under threat from Zeus.
Artemis halts the fleet and requires Iphigenia because of Agamemnon’s offense or vow.
Artemis snatches Iphigenia away and replaces her with a deer.
Artemis immortalizes Iphigenia after substituting an animal or phantom.
Artemis transports her to the Tauri and appoints her priestess.
The cult title Artemis Iphigeneia associates or compounds Iphigenia with Artemis.
Roman tradition equates Iphigenia with Diana in the Arician cult complex.
Iphigenia becomes Hecate by Artemis’s will in Hesiodic and Stesichorean testimony.
Athena commands Thoas to release Iphigenia, Orestes, and their companions.
Athena assigns Iphigenia to serve Artemis at Brauron and foretells her burial.

god_relations.myth: Orestes sent to recover the Taurian image
god_relations.note: Apollo’s oracle sends Orestes to Tauris, indirectly causing their reunion and escape.
A scholiastic genealogical variant makes Ares Ixion’s father.
Through Lapithes, Diodorus’s genealogy gives Ixion remote descent from Apollo.
Zeus receives the polluted suppliant, purifies him, and admits him to divine favor.
Zeus fashions a cloud resembling Hera to expose Ixion’s illicit desire.
Zeus imposes Ixion’s endless punishment for ingratitude and his offense against Hera.
Ixion illicitly approaches or attempts to rape Hera while enjoying Zeus’s favor.
In later accounts Hera reports Ixion’s advance and helps expose his offense.
god_relations.source: Pseudo-Apollodorus; Lucian, Dialogues of the Gods 6

god_relations.note: Hermes restrains or binds Ixion to the wheel at Zeus’s command.
Ares helps restrain Ixion in the early Classical wheel-binding scene.
Athena carries Ixion’s punitive wheel in the Attic kantharos scene.
Later visual interpretations sometimes make Hephaestus the wheel’s smith or punitive agent.
god_relations.source: South Italian, Etruscan, and Roman art

god_relations.note: Later tradition relocates Ixion’s wheel to Hades’s realm without direct dialogue.

god_relations.myth: Orpheus performs before the underworld rulers
god_relations.note: She is present as underworld queen when Orpheus’s performance halts Ixion’s punishment.
An Erinys binds Ixion to his wheel in the earliest secure infernal localization.
Chiron raises Jason and gives him his name.
Hera saves the Argo because Jason is dear to her.
Jason carries the disguised Hera across the river and loses one sandal.

god_relations.myth: Building and voyage of the Argo
god_relations.note: Athena directs the Argo’s construction and helps Jason’s ship through the Symplegades.
Athena attends Jason as the serpent disgorges him in a unique vase image.
Jason sacrifices to Apollo Embasios before the Argo sails.
Jason dedicates an image or shrine to Artemis during the return voyage.
Aphrodite gives Jason the iynx spell that inflames Medea’s desire.
Jason performs Medea’s prescribed nocturnal rite to Hecate before using the drug.
The Libyan god assists Jason and the stranded Argonauts and gives guidance or a clod.
Heracles refuses command in Jason’s favor and joins his expedition.
Heracles rebukes Jason and the crew for lingering with the Lemnian women.
Castor sails as a companion under Jason’s command.
Talos opposes Jason’s returning ship and is destroyed by Medea.
Circe purifies Jason and Medea from the pollution of Apsyrtus’s killing.
Laocoön serves Apollo as his priest in Hyginus and Servius.
Apollo sends serpents after Laocoön violates his prohibition against marriage and procreation.
Laocoön and his children are killed after his sexual sacrilege before Apollo’s image.
Apollo sends two serpents as a sign; they kill Laocoön’s sons but not him.
Laocoön is chosen as Neptune’s priest and sacrifices a bull when attacked.
Sophocles’ fragment places an invocation of Poseidon within Laocoön’s story.
Athena blinds Laocoön and summons serpents that kill his sons.
The serpents shelter beneath Minerva’s image, prompting belief that Laocoön was divinely punished.
Artemis appears beside Apollo while Laocoön’s household suffers the serpent attack.

god_relations.myth: Zeus approaches Leda disguised as a swan
god_relations.note: Zeus assumes a swan’s form and gains sexual access through deception.

god_relations.myth: Nemesis lays Helen’s egg for Leda to foster
god_relations.note: Nemesis bears Helen’s egg, which is delivered to Leda for custody.

god_relations.myth: Leda is deified under Nemesis’s name
god_relations.note: A late Christian account claims Leda became Nemesis after death.
Leda bears Castor to Tyndareus.
Homer makes Polydeuces the son of Leda and Tyndareus.
Later genealogy makes Polydeuces the son of Leda and Zeus.
Some traditions place Phoebe among Leda’s daughters or Tyndarid family.
Diodorus rationalizes Hecate as Medea's mortal mother by Aeëtes.
Medea invokes or serves Hecate in Hellenistic and Roman accounts.
Medea is Helios's granddaughter through Aeëtes.
Helios supplies his granddaughter with the chariot used to escape Corinth.
Circe is Medea's aunt in the Hesiodic solar genealogy.
Circe purifies Medea and Jason of blood guilt, then rebukes and expels them.
Hera engineers Medea's passion so her aid to Jason will destroy Pelias.
Medea uses Hera's sanctuary for her children and establishes their rites.
Athena joins Hera in seeking Aphrodite's help to manipulate Medea.
At Hera and Athena's request, Aphrodite persuades Eros to inflame Medea.
Aphrodite teaches Jason the charm that secures Medea's assistance.
Medea destroys Crete's bronze guardian through hostile visions and enchantment.
In one variant Medea offers immortality, then removes Talos's vein nail.
Zeus requires Medea and Jason to undergo purification for Apsyrtus's murder.
Themis communicates Zeus's purification command to Hera; Medea receives it indirectly.
Thetis helps the Argo under Hera's orders while Medea is aboard.
Apollo reveals Anaphe and saves the voyagers; Medea joins the resulting rites.
Dionysus asks Medea to restore his nurses to youth.
Later mythographers make Ares Meleager's biological father.
The Hesiodic Catalogue calls Meleager loved of Ares.
Artemis sends the boar whose death and trophies bring catastrophe upon Meleager's family.
Apollo supports the Curetes and kills Meleager with arrows in an early variant.
Althaea invokes Hades to bring death upon Meleager.
Althaea invokes Persephone to bring death upon Meleager.
The night-wandering Erinys hears Althaea's curse against Meleager.
Castor hunts beside Meleager in early iconography.
Castor and Meleager sail together as Argonauts.
Polydeuces hunts beside Meleager in early iconography.
Polydeuces and Meleager sail together as Argonauts.
Heracles aims at Meleager's shade, then listens to him and weeps.
Heracles and the youthful Meleager belong to the Argonautic crew.
Eos is Memnon’s immortal mother.

god_relations.myth: Recovery and mourning after Memnon’s death
god_relations.note: Eos recovers or mourns Memnon’s body after Achilles kills him.
Eos petitions Zeus and obtains immortality for Memnon.
Zeus weighs the destinies of Memnon and Achilles before their duel.
Zeus grants Eos’ request that Memnon receive immortality.
In Ovid, Jupiter grants commemorative birds in response to Aurora’s grief.
Their divine mothers plead on opposing sides while the heroes’ fates are weighed.
Hermes holds the scales weighing Memnon’s and Achilles’ fates in some vase scenes.
Memnon wears divine armor fashioned by Hephaestus.
The rising Sun awakens Memnon’s statue, whose voice salutes Eos.
Through marriage to Zeus’ daughter Helen, Menelaus is Zeus’ son-in-law.
Zeus oversees Menelaus’ duel with Paris and the subsequent broken treaty.
Castor is Helen’s brother and therefore Menelaus’ brother-in-law.
Aphrodite frustrates Menelaus’ victory by removing Paris from his grip.
Aphrodite restrains Menelaus’ anger and prevents him from killing Helen.
Athena deflects Pandarus’ arrow so that Menelaus receives a nonfatal wound.
Executing Zeus’ plan, Athena induces the shot that wounds Menelaus.
Hera supports Menelaus and the Achaeans against Paris and Troy.
Hermes transports the real Helen to Egypt, where Menelaus later recovers her.
Menelaus and his companions seize and hold the shape-changing sea god.
Proteus gives Menelaus ritual instructions, return directions, and prophecies.
The Egyptian king safeguards Helen and Menelaus’ treasure, then restores both.
Menelaus is sacrificed to Artemis through Iphigenia in a late variant.
Hyginus names the Mother Goddess as Midas' mother by Tmolus.
Later mythography synthesizes Cybele and Gordias as Midas' parents.
Midas reportedly dedicates his royal judgment-throne at Apollo's Delphi.
Apollo gives Midas ass's ears for rejecting the musical verdict.
Midas prefers Marsyas during Apollo's alternate musical contest.
Midas hosts Silenus and returns him to Dionysus.
Dionysus grants Midas the disastrous power to turn touched objects gold.
Dionysus instructs Midas how to relinquish the golden touch.
After renouncing wealth, Midas follows Pan in the countryside.
Midas alone rejects Tmolus' verdict and prefers Pan's pipes.
Hyginus names Pan as an alternate opponent of Apollo.
Hermes leads or restrains bound Silenus before the enthroned Midas.
An uncertain Iris or Eileithyia-like goddess appears behind Midas.
Zeus' sanctuary at Ancyra reportedly preserved the anchor found by Midas.
Zeus is Minos’s divine father.
Minos periodically consults Zeus and derives his laws from the god.

god_relations.myth: Ring challenge aboard the tribute ship
god_relations.note: Zeus answers Minos’s invocation with lightning during his contest with Theseus.
Europa bears Minos to Zeus.
Pasiphae is Minos’s wife and mother of his principal children.
Poseidon sends Minos a magnificent bull after Minos prays for a divine sign.
Poseidon punishes Minos’s broken sacrifice vow by afflicting Pasiphae with desire for the bull.
A late variant makes Aphrodite cause Pasiphae’s desire as punishment involving Minos’s household.
Amphitrite supports Theseus and gives him gifts, enabling him to defeat Minos’s test.
The Nereids receive Theseus in the sea during Minos’s challenge.
Ariadne is Minos’s daughter.
Minos guards or confines Ariadne before she aids Theseus and flees Crete.
Glaucus is Minos’s son by Pasiphae.
Minos compels Polyidus to find and revive his dead son Glaucus.
Minos confines Pasiphae’s bull-headed child in the labyrinth and supplies it the Athenian tribute.
Scylla falls in love with Minos and betrays her father and city for him.
Minos rejects Scylla and, in some versions, ties her to his ship or has her drowned.
Juno restricts Echo to repeating others' concluding words.
Echo distracts Juno while Jupiter's nymph companions escape discovery.
Nemesis makes Narcissus love an image he cannot possess.
Hermes points out Narcissus among the beautiful dead.
Selene is Narcissus' mother in the Latmian genealogy.
Pan drives pastoral people mad, causing them to dismember Echo.
Pan embraces Echo and teaches her to reproduce songs.
Pan repeatedly pursues Echo, but she successfully evades him.
The Muses teach Echo music.
The Muses preserve Echo's imitative voice after her bodily destruction.
Earth conceals Echo's scattered limbs after her dismemberment.
Narcissus' pool has Bacchic associations, but no direct encounter occurs.
Thetis is Neoptolemus’ divine grandmother through Achilles.
Thetis warns Neoptolemus to return from Troy overland.
The Aeacid genealogy makes Neoptolemus a descendant of Zeus.
Neoptolemus kills Priam at Zeus Herkeios’ household altar.
Neoptolemus challenges Apollo over Achilles’ death or attacks his sanctuary.
Apollo’s hostility brings Neoptolemus to a fatal end at Delphi.
After death Neoptolemus remains in Apollo’s precinct overseeing heroic rites.

god_relations.myth: Heracles orders the journey to Troy
god_relations.note: Heracles’ epiphany commands Neoptolemus and Philoctetes to sail to Troy.
Neoptolemus joins the horse operation conducted under Athena’s protection.
Poseidon fathered Neleus, making Nestor his mortal grandson.
Nestor presides over a communal sacrifice of eighty-one bulls to Poseidon.
Later genealogists place Nestor in the Aeolid line through Cretheus and Neleus.
The cup’s verse invokes Aphrodite as the source of immediate erotic desire.
Later tradition says Apollo granted Nestor years taken from Chloris’ Niobid relatives.
Nestor hosts Athena disguised as Mentor and recognizes her divine departure.
After recognizing Athena, Nestor arranges a sacrifice in her honor.
Heracles destroys Pylos and Nestor survives the slaughter of Neleus’ other sons.
Zeus halts Nestor and Diomedes with a thunderbolt during their counterattack.
Apollo kills Niobe's sons with arrows after her comparison with Leto.
Artemis kills Niobe's daughters with arrows; Roman sources call her Diana.
Sappho says Leto and Niobe were once dearest companions.
Niobe claims superiority through lineage and numerous children and disparages Leto.
Leto urges Apollo and Artemis to avenge Niobe's insult by killing her children.
Zeus turns the people to stone, leaving Niobe's children unburied nine days.
Zeus grants Niobe's prayer to be transformed into stone.
As Amphion's father, Zeus is Niobe's father-in-law in the dominant genealogy.
Modern writers hypothesized that Sipylian Niobe was Cybele, but ancient evidence does not establish the equation.
After confrontation and oath, Circe becomes Odysseus' lover and host.
Circe restores his men and advises him about Hades and sea hazards.
Calypso compulsorily keeps Odysseus seven years and offers immortality.
Under divine command, Calypso releases Odysseus and helps his departure.
Aeolus hosts Odysseus and gives him the winds in a bag.
Odysseus invokes Apollo before beginning the suitors' slaughter.
Ares supports the Brygians against Odysseus until Athena intervenes.
Athena is Odysseus' principal divine patron, adviser, protector, and battlefield ally.
In later drama Athena's favor decides the armor contest for Odysseus.
Athena disguises Odysseus as an old beggar and later restores him.
Athena stops renewed civil violence and secures peace on Ithaca.
Odysseus twice evades Charybdis' destructive whirlpool.
After the crew kills his cattle, Helios demands punishment of Odysseus' expedition.
Odysseus encounters the image or shade of Heracles among the dead.
Heracles appears and commands the resolution opposed by Odysseus' earlier scheme.
Hermes gives Odysseus moly and instructions for overcoming Circe.
Odysseus blinds Polyphemus after the Cyclops eats six crewmen.
Odysseus calls himself Nobody and escapes beneath Polyphemus' sheep.
After Odysseus reveals his name, Polyphemus invokes Poseidon's vengeance.
Poseidon obstructs Odysseus' return and wrecks his raft.
Odysseus must travel inland and sacrifice to reconcile with Poseidon.
Odysseus arms himself but cannot prevent Scylla killing six companions.
Odysseus hears their promised knowledge while bound safely to the mast.
Zeus destroys Odysseus' ship after the crew slaughters Helios' cattle.
Zeus permits Athena's aid and sanctions peace after the suitors' deaths.

god_relations.myth: Oracles of patricide, incest, and pollution
god_relations.note: Apollo predicts Oedipus’s crimes and commands investigation of Laius’s unpunished murder.
Zeus’s thunder signals that Oedipus’s destined death has arrived.
Oedipus’s Erinys carries familial ruin into his sons’ mutual destruction.

god_relations.myth: Arrival in the sacred grove at Colonus
god_relations.note: Oedipus enters their grove, prays to them, and gains his destined resting place.
Oedipus invokes Athena’s city and territory without meeting her personally.
Oedipus’s promised grave enters the Colonus landscape sacred to Poseidon.
Oedipus’s rejected corpse is secretly buried within Demeter’s precinct.
Oedipus speaks of entering Hades, but no direct meeting is narrated.
Oedipus defeats the Sphinx by answering her riddle; she then destroys herself.
Orestes obeys Apollo’s command to kill his father’s murderers.
Apollo purifies Orestes, directs his flight, and defends him at trial.
Apollo sends Orestes to Tauris to retrieve Artemis’ image.
Apollo ends the crisis and assigns Orestes’ trial and marriage.
Hermes warns Aegisthus that Orestes will avenge Agamemnon.
Orestes invokes chthonic Hermes while preparing his revenge.
Orestes invokes Zeus in pursuing vengeance for Agamemnon.
Athena establishes the court, votes for Orestes, and secures his acquittal.
Athena stops pursuit and directs Orestes to install Artemis’ image.
The Erinyes pursue Orestes for shedding his mother’s blood.
The Erinyes prosecute Orestes before Athena’s homicide court.
Their black forms afflict Orestes until his finger sacrifice brings recovery.
Orestes removes Artemis’ cult image from Tauris on Apollo’s orders.
The Dioscuri condemn Apollo’s command and prescribe settlements for Orestes.
Orestes sacrifices to the Graces alongside the cured-form Eumenides.
Some later genealogies make Apollo the biological father of Orpheus.

god_relations.myth: Apollo sends the father of songs
god_relations.note: Apollo serves as Orpheus’s patron or sender, without necessarily being his father.
Orpheus abandons Dionysus and worships Apollo as the greatest god.
In the printed operatic ending, Apollo takes Orpheus heavenward.
The Muses patronize Orpheus, mourn him, gather his remains, and bury him.
Orpheus teaches or performs initiatory rites associated with Dionysus.
Dionysus sends Dionysiac women to dismember Orpheus after his devotion to Apollo.
Bacchus avenges Orpheus by turning the Ciconian murderers into trees.
Orpheus charms and petitions Hades, who conditionally releases his wife.
Orpheus moves Persephone with song, and she participates in releasing his wife.
Hermes escorts or reclaims Eurydice as Orpheus loses her again.
Modern Hadestown makes Hermes the narrator associated closely with Orpheus.
Chiron advises Jason to include Orpheus in the Argonautic expedition.
Heracles and Orpheus serve together among the Argonauts.
Castor is Orpheus’s fellow Argonaut and participates in Orpheus-led rites or songs.
Orpheus overwhelms the Sirens’ song with his own and saves the crew.
Aphrodite rescues Butes after Orpheus’s counter-song fails to retain him.
Proteus narrates Orpheus’s story to Aristaeus but never meets Orpheus directly.
A euhemerizing account makes Orpheus learn rites associated with the Mother.
Orpheus transmits rites associated with Cybele after learning them.
Pseudepigrapha present Orpheus as authoritative revealer of Demeter’s wanderings and rites.
Orpheus invokes and ritually engages Hecate during his late-antique Argonautic narrative.
One reported tradition says Zeus kills Orpheus for revealing mysteries to humans.
The infernal Furies weep for the first time when moved by Orpheus’s song.
Orpheus’s music persuades Charon to grant him passage into the underworld.
Orpheus pacifies the underworld guardian with his music.
Orpheus greets Helios at dawn, worshipping the sun as Apollo.
Palamedes descends from Poseidon through the elder Nauplius in the systematized genealogy.
Poseidon and the Fates execute vengeance for Palamedes through the Greek fleet’s destruction.
Palamedes dedicates the dice he invented in Tyche’s sanctuary at Argos.
Zeus orders Pandora’s manufacture as retaliation for humanity receiving stolen fire.

god_relations.myth: Zeus’s punishment for Prometheus’s stolen fire
god_relations.note: Zeus designs Pandora as a destructive gift whose arrival permanently changes human life.
Hephaestus forms Pandora from earth and water, giving her voice and strength.
Hephaestus makes the extraordinary golden crown worn by the unnamed maiden.
Athena clothes and adorns Pandora during her divine preparation.
Athena teaches Pandora the craft of weaving.
Hyginus says Minerva gives life to the clay figure made by Vulcan.
Aphrodite gives Pandora charm, painful longing, and cares that consume the limbs.

god_relations.myth: Hermes gives Pandora her character and speech
god_relations.note: Hermes installs a shameless mind, deceitful character, lies, and crafty speech.
Hermes names her Pandora because the Olympians gave her as a gift.
Hermes acts as herald and delivers Pandora to Epimetheus.
The Charites and Peitho place golden necklaces upon Pandora.
The Horae crown Pandora with flowers of spring.
Epimetheus accepts Pandora despite Prometheus’s warning and recognizes the evil afterward.
Later mythographers make Pandora the partner or wife of Epimetheus.

god_relations.myth: Epimetheus opens the jar of evils
god_relations.note: Philodemus reports a variant in which Epimetheus, rather than Pandora, opens the jar.
His fire theft occasions Pandora’s creation, and he warns Epimetheus against Zeus’s gifts.
A scholium glosses Pandora as Earth, giver of everything necessary for life.
Iris appears as an onlooker in a vase scene depicting Pandora’s creation.
Paris awards Aphrodite victory after she promises him Helen.
Aphrodite promises Paris marriage with Helen and encourages his expedition.
Aphrodite breaks Paris's helmet strap and transports him from the duel.
Paris rejects Hera's claim and offer in favor of Aphrodite.
Hera sends a storm against Paris as he sails with Helen.
Paris rejects Athena's claim and offer in favor of Aphrodite.
Hostile Athena manipulates Pandarus, preventing Paris's defeat from ending the war.
Hermes conducts the three goddesses to Paris on Zeus's order.
Zeus refuses to judge the goddesses and delegates the decision to Paris.
Eris creates the dispute that ultimately forces Paris to judge the goddesses.
Apollo and Paris jointly kill Achilles near the Scaean gates.
In Roman accounts, Apollo directs Paris's arrow against Achilles.
Hyginus makes Apollo assume Paris's appearance when Achilles is killed.

god_relations.myth: Divine plan for the Trojan War
god_relations.note: Themis helps Zeus plan the war sequence in which Paris becomes instrumental.
Thetis's wedding provides the setting for the quarrel Paris later judges.
Heracles' inherited bow and poison enable Philoctetes to kill Paris.
Proteus detains Helen and her treasure and sends Paris away empty-handed.
Menoetius is consistently named as Patroclus’ father.
Apollo repeatedly repels Patroclus, warns him, then strikes and strips him.

god_relations.myth: Apollo incites Hector disguised as Asius
god_relations.note: Apollo assumes Asius’ appearance while directing Hector back toward Patroclus.
Zeus grants only part of Achilles’ prayer and ordains Patroclus’ death sequence.
Thetis mourns Patroclus and preserves his corpse with ambrosia and nectar.

god_relations.myth: Transmission of healing remedies through Achilles
god_relations.note: Patroclus learns remedies from Achilles, who had learned them from Chiron.
Iris carries Achilles’ request to the winds so Patroclus’ pyre burns.
Boreas answers the prayer and fans Patroclus’ pyre.
Zephyrus acts with Boreas to fan Patroclus’ pyre.
Hephaestus made the urn eventually holding Patroclus’ and Achilles’ bones.
Dionysus gave Thetis the urn eventually containing Patroclus’ bones.

god_relations.myth: Patroclus awaits burial among the dead
god_relations.note: Patroclus’ ghost remains excluded from Hades’ dead until cremation.
A variant makes Endeis Chiron’s daughter, making Peleus his grandson.
Chiron saves Peleus from the Centaurs and restores his hidden sword.
In the dominant Greek account, Chiron teaches Peleus to hold the transforming Thetis.

god_relations.myth: Wedding gift of the ash spear
god_relations.note: Chiron gives Peleus the Pelian ash spear later wielded by Achilles.
Peleus entrusts Achilles to Chiron for upbringing and instruction.
Peleus and the Dioscuri are fellow Argonauts in later expedition catalogues.
The Dioscuri join Peleus and Jason in the capture of Iolcus.
Heracles and Peleus appear together as members of the Argonautic expedition.
Thetis is Peleus’ divine wife and the mother of Achilles.
Peleus restrains the resisting Thetis through her transformations until she submits to marriage.
Thetis and the Nereids guide Peleus’ ship through the dangerous Planctae.
Thetis intercedes with Psamathe and ends the destruction of Peleus’ herds.
Thetis promises to release Peleus from mortality and receive him as a sea-divinity.
Nereus is Thetis’ father and therefore Peleus’ divine father-in-law.
The Nereids flee or witness Peleus’ violent seizure of their sister Thetis.
The Nereids help guide the Argo safely while Thetis appears to Peleus.
The sea-nymphs escort immortalized Peleus to his dwelling beneath the sea.
Zeus approves or sponsors Thetis’ mortal marriage after learning the dangerous-son prophecy.
Zeus participates in the divine assembly associated with Peleus’ wedding.
Later accounts credit Poseidon with giving Peleus the immortal horses Xanthus and Balius.
Themis proposes Peleus as Thetis’ mortal husband after revealing her son’s destined superiority.
Eris initiates the divine beauty dispute during Peleus’ wedding celebration.
Hera attends Peleus’ wedding and becomes a contestant in Eris’ beauty dispute.
Athena attends Peleus’ wedding and competes in the ensuing beauty judgment.
Aphrodite attends Peleus’ wedding and ultimately wins the resulting judgment of Paris.
Later scholia list Aphrodite among deities who give Peleus a wedding present.
Hermes conducts the rival goddesses from Peleus’ wedding dispute to Paris.
Later wedding catalogues make Hephaestus a guest and giver of weaponry to Peleus.
Apollo attends and sings at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis.
The Muses sing during the divine celebration of Peleus’ marriage.
Dionysus appears among the divine guests processing to Peleus’ wedding.
In Ovid’s Roman variant, Proteus advises Peleus how to bind the changing Thetis.
Zeus ultimately gives Pelops the royal sceptre through Hermes.
Zeus stands centrally between Pelops and Oenomaus before their race.
Later genealogy makes Pelops Zeus’s descendant through Tantalus.
Hephaestus purifies Pelops after the killing of Myrtilus.
Hermes hands Zeus’s royal sceptre to Pelops.
One later variant assigns Pelops’s restoration to Hermes.
Poseidon loves and abducts Pelops, receiving him as his beloved.
Pelops becomes Poseidon’s intimate attendant in the divine dwelling.
Poseidon gives Pelops a golden chariot and tireless winged horses.
Pelops invokes Aphrodite’s reciprocal charis when recalling Poseidon’s love.
Clotho draws restored Pelops from the cauldron with an ivory shoulder.
In later versions, grieving Demeter consumes part of Pelops’s shoulder.
Demeter afflicts Greece with barrenness after Pelops dismembers Stymphalus.
Some later accounts make Rhea reconstitute Pelops after his dismemberment.
Some accounts associate Pelops’s purification with the river-god Oceanus.
Pausanias treats Heracles as Pelops’s fourth-generation descendant.
Heracles assigns Pelops the Pelopion and sacrifices to him in a pit.
Heracles establishes the Olympic precinct beside Pelops’s tomb.
Athena protects Penelope’s household and advances Odysseus’s return.
Athena sends Iphthime’s likeness to console Penelope about Telemachus.
Athena puts Penelope to sleep and enhances her beauty.
Athena keeps Penelope asleep and away from the suitors’ slaughter.
Penelope prays for Artemis to kill her rather than force remarriage.
Penelope invokes Zeus and remains within the settlement he authorizes.
Hermes fathers Pan by Penelope in a non-Homeric genealogy.
Penelope bears Pan to Hermes in Herodotus’s genealogy.
Apollodorus makes Penelope Pan’s mother after her expulsion to Mantinea.
Duris makes Pan the child of Penelope and all the suitors.
Servian and scholastic traditions make Pan Penelope and Odysseus’s son.
Apollo reportedly fathers Pan by a Penelope, possibly Odysseus’s wife.
Circe receives Penelope and makes her immortal.
Penthesilea is consistently named as the war-god's daughter.
Ares gives his daughter armor for her Trojan campaign.

god_relations.myth: Ares attempts vengeance after her death
god_relations.note: Ares tries to attack the Greeks after Penthesilea dies.
Eris gives Penthesilea her double-bladed battle-axe or halberd.
The Erinyes pursue Penthesilea and drive her to seek purification.
Aphrodite beautifies her dead body, awakening remorseful love in Achilles.
Zeus uses thunderbolts to stop Ares attacking her Greek killers.
Pentheus and Dionysus are maternal first cousins.
Pentheus denies Dionysus’ divinity, suppresses his rites, and imprisons his disguised manifestation.

god_relations.myth: Pentheus disguised and led to Cithaeron
god_relations.note: Dionysus deceives, feminizes, and leads Pentheus to spy upon the maenads.
Dionysus exposes Pentheus to the maddened maenads and causes his dismemberment.
Dionysus punishes Pentheus for denying his divinity and persecuting his worship.
Pentheus denies or mocks Zeus’ paternity of Dionysus; Zeus never confronts him directly.
Harmonia is Pentheus’ maternal grandmother.
Zeus impregnates Danaë in golden form and fathers Perseus.
Danaë is Perseus’ mother.
Mother and infant share confinement, sea exposure, and exile on Seriphos.
Perseus protects or avenges Danaë by destroying her coercive ruler.
Hermes guides Perseus and facilitates his acquisition of the curved blade.
Hermes supplies Perseus with an adamantine sickle or curved sword.
Perseus sacrifices to Mercury after killing the sea creature.
Perseus uses the invisibility cap belonging to or originating from Hades.
Hephaestus fashions the represented image of Perseus on Heracles’ shield.
Perseus intercepts Enyo’s shared eye to compel directions to the nymphs.
The nymphs give Perseus the kibisis, winged sandals, and invisibility cap.
Perseus cuts off the mortal Gorgon’s head while avoiding her gaze.
Pegasus springs from Medusa’s severed neck when Perseus strikes.
Perseus uses Medusa’s head to transform Atlas into a mountain.
Perseus fights Dionysus or forces associated with his Argive invasion.
Perseus petrifies Ariadne during the late-antique conflict with Dionysus.
Hera encourages Perseus to resist Dionysus.
Hermes mediates the conflict between Perseus and Dionysus.
Perseus is Heracles’ ancestor through the Amphitryon and Alcmena lines.
Some scholarship proposes identification on eastern coinage, but individual cases remain contested.
The 2010 film makes Hades Perseus’ principal divine antagonist.
Helios is Phaethon's biological father in the principal charioteer genealogies.
Bound by his oath, Helios reluctantly grants Phaethon the chariot.

god_relations.myth: Instructions for driving the solar chariot
god_relations.note: Helios explains the route, dangers, horses, and proper handling of the reins.
Sol places the dead Phaethon among the stars.
Oceanus is Phaethon's maternal grandfather through Clymene.
Oceanus raises and plays with Phaethon, accidentally foreshadowing his watery death.
Tethys is Phaethon's maternal grandmother through Clymene.
Tethys recovers wreckage after Phaethon's catastrophic fall.
Zeus kills Phaethon with a thunderbolt to halt the burning of earth.
Phaethon's errant course burns Earth, who appeals to Zeus for intervention.

god_relations.myth: The Hours prepare the solar team
god_relations.note: The Hours yoke the immortal horses for Phaethon's departure.

god_relations.myth: Dawn opens the gates before Phaethon's ride
god_relations.note: Eos opens the dawn gates before Phaethon departs in the solar chariot.
In Nonnus, Eosphorus helps yoke or guide the team for Phaethon.
Selene attends Clymene's wedding and Phaethon's birth in Nonnus.
Philoctetes serves Heracles and, in some versions, lights his funeral pyre.
Heracles rewards Philoctetes with his bow, quiver, and poisoned arrows.
Philoctetes visits Chryse with Heracles and learns the location of its altar.
The deified Heracles commands Philoctetes to accept healing and fight at Troy.
Hera sends the snake that wounds Philoctetes for helping Heracles escape mortality.
Philoctetes is bitten near Apollo’s sacred altar or precinct at Chryse.
Philoctetes dedicates Heracles’ bow in Apollo’s South-Italian sanctuary.
Procne exploits Dionysus's rites and maenadic costume to rescue Philomela.
Hera punishes Aëdon and Polytechnus for claiming a happier marriage than hers.
Eris provokes the craftsmanship contest between Aëdon and Polytechnus at Hera's command.
Zeus stops the violence by transforming Aëdon, Chelidon, and their family into birds.

god_relations.myth: Achilles killed during Polyxena marriage negotiations
god_relations.note: Apollo’s Thymbraean sanctuary is the setting for negotiations over Polyxena and Achilles’ ambush.
Glaucus is listed among Priam's sons by other women.
A son named Hyperion appears in Apollodorus's Priamid catalog.
A daughter named Medusa appears in Apollodorus's Priamid catalog.
Hermes disguises himself, guides Priam safely, opens barriers, and escorts him home.
Iris conveys Zeus's command that Priam travel to ransom Hector.
Zeus protects Priam's mission and grants the favorable eagle omen he requests.
Heracles spares or releases Podarces after Hesione redeems him and permits his rule.
Hermes conducts Protesilaus from the underworld for his temporary reunion with Laodamia.
Protesilaus temporarily returns from the realm ruled by Hades, without a surviving personal exchange.
Later tradition credits nymphs with planting elms around Protesilaus's tomb.
Wordsworth individually assigns the ancient gods' collective permission for Protesilaus's return to Great Jove.
Pygmalion desires and has sex with her naked ivory cult image.
After Pygmalion sacrifices and prays, Venus animates his maiden and favors their marriage.
Pygmalion is Adonis’ maternal grandfather through Metharme and Cinyras.
Pygmalion is Adonis’ earlier ancestor through Paphos and Cinyras.
Pygmalion is possibly Poseidon’s son if Hyginus’ namesake is the Cypriot figure.
Rhadamanthus is the son of Zeus and Europa.

god_relations.myth: Appointment as judge of the dead
god_relations.note: Zeus appoints Rhadamanthus to judge the souls of Asia.
Europa is Rhadamanthus’s mother in the dominant genealogy.
A divergent genealogy makes Rhadamanthus the son of Hephaestus.
A divergent genealogy makes Rhadamanthus the grandson of Talos.
Ibycus reportedly called Rhadamanthus Talos’s lover; Talos’s identity is uncertain.

god_relations.myth: Removal of Alcmene to the Blessed Isles
god_relations.note: Hermes brings Alcmene to Rhadamanthus at Zeus’s command.
A late and disputed tradition makes Rhadamanthus Heracles’s archery teacher.
Rhadamanthus exercises judicial authority within the realm of Hades.
Aeacus is the son of Zeus and Aegina.
Aeacus intercedes with Zeus, whose response ends the drought afflicting Greece.
A weak late variant makes Europa the mother of Aeacus.
Apollo summons Aeacus to build Troy’s wall and interprets the snake omen.
Aeacus builds Troy’s fortification alongside Poseidon and Apollo.
Chiron is Aeacus’s father-in-law in a competing genealogy of Endeis.
Aeacus angrily recalls Heracles stealing Cerberus from the underworld.
Juno devastates Aeacus’s island with plague from jealousy of Aegina.
Aeacus serves as judge or gatekeeper within the realm of Hades.
After death Aeacus sits in honour beside Persephone and Pluto.
Aeacus mistakes the disguised Dionysus for Heracles and threatens punishment.
Apollo’s oracle directs the Greeks to seek Aeacus as their intercessor.
Zeus fathers the Trojan-war Sarpedon on Laodamia.
Zeus fathers the Europa-Sarpedon who also fights at Troy.
Zeus grants Sarpedon a lifespan extending across three generations.
Zeus mourns Sarpedon, sends blood rain, and orders his body's preservation and return.
A Christian-era variant makes Zeus father Sarpedon with Hippodamia.
Europa is Sarpedon's mother in Hesiodic and Aeschylean tradition.

god_relations.myth: Lycian expedition and defense of Sarpedon's corpse
god_relations.note: Glaucus co-leads the Lycians, fights beside Sarpedon, and rallies defenders around his corpse.
Hera dissuades Zeus from removing Sarpedon alive from his fated death.
Apollo retrieves, washes, anoints, and clothes Sarpedon's body at Zeus' command.
Hypnos and Thanatos carry Sarpedon's prepared body home to Lycia.
Thanatos and Hypnos carry Sarpedon's prepared body home to Lycia.
Hermes supervises Hypnos and Thanatos carrying Sarpedon's corpse, an addition absent from Homer.
Zeus loves Semele and fathers Dionysus with her.
Zeus’s lightning and divine splendor burn the pregnant Semele.
Semele bears Dionysus after conceiving him by Zeus.
Dionysus retrieves Semele from Hades, renames her Thyone, and ascends.
Dionysus returns to punish the family that denied his mother’s divine pregnancy.
Disguised Hera persuades Semele to demand Zeus’s lethal marital splendor.
Harmonia is Semele’s mother in the standard Theban genealogy.
Artemis causes Actaeon’s death to prevent his proposed marriage to Semele.
Semele descends from Aphrodite through her mother Harmonia.
Aphrodite helps set Zeus’s passion for Semele in motion.
Semele descends from Ares through her mother Harmonia.
Semele resides in Hades’s realm until Dionysus retrieves her.
The Muses sing hymns as Semele’s shade ascends toward divine status.

god_relations.myth: Invocation before the assault on Thebes
god_relations.note: The expedition invokes martial destruction and symbolically claims Ares’ favor.
Aeolus is Sisyphus's father.
Glaucus is Sisyphus's son and dynastic successor.
Sisyphus obeys the Nereids' direction to honor dead Melicertes.
Sisyphus reveals that Zeus abducted Aegina, provoking divine anger.
Zeus sends Thanatos against Sisyphus after the abduction secret is disclosed.
Sisyphus tricks and binds personified Death, temporarily preventing human deaths.
Sisyphus overpowers and imprisons Thanatos when Death is sent against him.
Ares frees Thanatos and delivers Sisyphus because battles no longer cause deaths.
Sisyphus persuades Persephone to release him, then refuses to return voluntarily.
Persephone permits Sisyphus to leave Hades temporarily after hearing his plea.
Later art sometimes shows Hades observing Sisyphus laboring with his stone.
Hermes appears beside Sisyphus, plausibly escorting him back to Hades.
Cerberus and Sisyphus co-appear in underworld imagery without narrative interaction.
Heracles and Sisyphus co-appear in underworld art without conversing or fighting.
Zeus is Tantalus’s father in the dominant genealogy.
Zeus suspends a great stone above Tantalus for stealing divine food.
Zeus crushes or overturns Tantalus after his perjury about the dog.
Poseidon attends Tantalus’s banquet and carries Pelops away to Olympus.
Tantalus serves Pelops to Demeter, who unknowingly eats his shoulder.
Tantalus falsely denies to Hermes that he received Zeus’s stolen dog.
One variant makes Rhea the owner or beneficiary of Tantalus’s concealed dog.
One variant makes Hephaestus the maker or owner of the golden dog.
Disguised as Mentes and Mentor, she guides and emboldens his journey.
She assists Telemachus’ faction in battle and imposes peace.
Zeus authorizes Athena’s plan, sends omens, and sanctions peace affecting Telemachus.
Telemachus attends the Pylians’ sacrifice to Poseidon without meeting him.
Hermes is Telemachus’ remote ancestor through Autolycus and Anticleia.
Proteus indirectly supplies Telemachus with news through Menelaus’ embedded narrative.
After Odysseus’ death, Telemachus marries Circe.
Circe makes Telemachus immortal after Telegonus brings him to her island.
Telemachus kills Circe in Tzetzes’ post-Odyssean continuation.
Telemachus only hears that Calypso detains Odysseus; they never meet in Homer.
Fénelon invents extensive encounters between Telemachus and Calypso.
Poseidon is Theseus’s divine father in the double-conception tradition.
Poseidon receives Theseus in his palace, confirming his divine paternity.
Poseidon grants Theseus curses, one fatally invoked against Hippolytus.
Some traditions make Theseus Heracles’s companion during the Amazon expedition.
Heracles frees Theseus from his imprisonment in Hades.
Theseus protects the devastated Heracles and brings him to Athens.
Amphitrite welcomes Theseus and gives him a wreath and purple mantle.
Zeus answers Minos’s invocation with lightning during his contest with Theseus.
Theseus kills the Minotaur by varying methods in visual and literary traditions.
Ariadne is Theseus’s lover or intended wife in the Cretan cycle.
Ariadne gives Theseus the means to retrace his path from the Labyrinth.
Theseus abandons Ariadne because his love for Aegle overcomes him.
Theseus loses Ariadne when Artemis kills her following Dionysus’s accusation.
Dionysus orders or compels Theseus to abandon Ariadne, sometimes through a dream.
Dionysus’s accusation causes Artemis to kill Ariadne before Theseus can marry her.
Artemis kills Ariadne while Theseus is bringing her toward Athens.
Artemis reveals Hippolytus’s innocence to Theseus after the fatal curse.
Theseus presents the captured Marathonian bull for sacrifice to Apollo.
Theseus consults Apollo’s Delphic oracle in the developed biography.
Theseus honors Athens’s patroness through civic institutions and the Synoecia.
Aphrodite’s punishment of Hippolytus draws Theseus into his family’s catastrophe.
Castor attacks Attica to recover Helen and is wounded in one cyclic version.
Theseus accompanies Peirithous’s attempted abduction of Persephone from Hades.
Hades traps Theseus and Peirithous on a chair or rock.
Persephone preserves Tiresias’s intelligence while other dead remain witless shades.
Circe directs Odysseus to Tiresias, though they never meet directly.
Tiresias explains Poseidon’s hostility and prescribes a distant sacrifice.
Tiresias warns Odysseus not to harm Helios’s sacred cattle.
Callimachus says Hades will recognize and honour Tiresias after death.
Tiresias supports Zeus’s claim that women receive greater sexual pleasure.
Zeus compensates Tiresias with prophecy and prolonged life.
Tiresias rejects Hera’s position in her dispute with Zeus.
Hera blinds Tiresias after his verdict supports Zeus.
Tiresias accepts Dionysus’s divinity and prepares to join his rites.
Tiresias foretells Heracles’s labours, victories, apotheosis, and marriage to Hebe.
Tiresias explains that Ares requires payment for the slain dragon.
The conquerors intend Tiresias or Manto as a dedication to Apollo.
Apollo successively alters Tiresias’s sex or form in an extravagant variant.
Hera successively alters Tiresias’s sex or form in an extravagant variant.
Zeus successively alters Tiresias’s sex or form in an extravagant variant.
The Muses alter Tiresias’s sex or form in an extravagant variant.
Aphrodite alters Tiresias’s sex or form in an extravagant variant.
A fragmentary genealogical tradition may make Apollo Trophonius’ father.
Pausanias endorses the local belief that Trophonius was Apollo’s son.
Trophonius and Agamedes construct the threshold after Apollo lays foundations.
Apollo grants the brothers painless death as the best human reward.
Their coordinated oracles defer the decisive answer about children to Apollo.
Consultants sacrifice to Apollo while preparing to consult Trophonius.
Lebadeians regarded Demeter Europa as Trophonius’ nurse.
Cult and inscriptions explicitly identify Trophonius with Zeus Trophonios.
Her spring and throne enable consultants to remember Trophonius’ revelations.
Trophonius’ Praxitelean cult image was made in Asclepius’ likeness.
A Roman learned genealogy identifies cave-dwelling Mercury with Trophonius.

Abas.note: Abas is one of Diomedes’ companions transformed into a bird.

Acacallis.note: Acacallis is listed among Minos’s children by Pasiphae.

Academus.note: Academus reveals Helen’s hiding place to Theseus’s Dioscurid enemies.

Acamas.note: Acamas, son of Theseus and Phaedra, is Hippolytus’ paternal half-brother.
Acamas is a son of Theseus and Phaedra.

Acamas son of Eussorus.note: Ajax kills Acamas, son of Eussorus.

Acastus.note: Pelias’ son secretly joins and sails with the company.
Acastus, Pelias’s son, joins Jason’s crew in many Argonaut lists.
Jason gives Iolcus to Acastus after Pelias’s death.
In a divergent tradition, Acastus expels Jason and Medea from Iolcus.
Meleager allegedly wins the javelin event at Acastus's or Pelias's games.
Acastus appears beside Meleager among the named hunters.
Acastus purifies Peleus after the accidental killing of Eurytion.
Acastus accepts his wife’s false claim that Peleus attempted to violate her.
Acastus hides Peleus’ sword and abandons him asleep among threatening Centaurs.
Peleus later attacks Acastus’ city with Jason and the Dioscuri.
Protesilaus's father-in-law orders his image burned, precipitating Laodamia's suicide.

Achates.note: Learned commentary preserves Achates as a variant killer of Protesilaus.

Acheloos.note: Acheloos receives worship on Amphiaraus’ divided altar at Oropos.
Homer locates the nearby nymphs' dancing grounds by Acheloos without personal interaction.

Achelous.note: The transforming river-god courts Deianira until Heracles defeats him for her hand.
Heracles wrestles shape-changing Achelous and breaks off one horn.
Achelous' image decorates the cave beside Narcissus' pool; they never interact.

Acmon.note: Acmon accompanies Diomedes in exile before Aphrodite transforms him into a bird.

Acoetes.note: Hyginus identifies Acoetes as Laocoön’s father.
Pentheus orders Acoetes imprisoned and tortured after rejecting his account of Dionysus.

Acrisius.note: Acrisius is Perseus’ maternal grandfather through Danaë.
Perseus accidentally kills Acrisius with a discus, fulfilling the oracle.

Actaeon's hounds.myth: Actaeon hunted by his own hounds
Actaeon's hounds.note: His maddened dogs mistake their transformed master for prey and tear him apart.
Actaeon raises and commands the hunting pack that later kills him.

Actor.note: In Homer’s Actorid genealogy, Actor is Patroclus’ paternal grandfather.

Acusilaus.note: Later genealogy names Acusilaus as a son by Penelope.

Adrastus, son of Polynices.note: This distinct namesake is Adrastus's grandson in later genealogies.

Aeantides.note: Aeantides sporadically appears among Ajax’s additional children.

Aeetes.note: Aeetes receives the other portion of the teeth Cadmus sows at Thebes.
Meleager kills King Aeetes in Diodorus' exceptional and incompatible variant.

Aegeoneus.note: Aegeoneus is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Aegeus.note: Aegeus swears to shelter Medea after her expulsion from Corinth.
Medea later marries Aegeus in the Athenian tradition.
Minos holds Aegeus responsible for Androgeus’s death and forces Athens to provide tribute.
Aegeus is Theseus’s standard civic and legal father.
Aegeus recognizes Theseus by his sword and prevents his poisoning.
Theseus’s unchanged sail causes Aegeus to believe him dead and leap.

Aegiale.note: Aegiale, usually identified as Diomedes's wife, is Adrastus's daughter.

Aegialeia.note: Aegialeia is Diomedes’ wife, though later sources vary her parentage.
Later tradition says Aegialeia rejects Diomedes or plots his death.

Aegialeus.note: Aegialeus is Adrastus's son in Classical Epigoni traditions.
Adrastus leads or accompanies the Epigoni alongside his son Aegialeus.

Aegialeus.myth: Aegialeus dies during the Epigoni campaign
Aegialeus.note: Adrastus mourns his son and gathers or carries his remains home.
Aegialeus campaigns beside Diomedes and dies during the successful expedition.

Aegina.note: The Aeacid genealogy makes Neoptolemus a descendant of Aegina.
Aegina is Aeacus’s mother in the dominant genealogy.
Sisyphus discloses the secret of Aegina's abduction to her father.

Aegisthus.note: Aegisthus is Agamemnon's dynastic enemy and adulterous rival.
In Homer, Aegisthus invites Agamemnon to a banquet and kills him.
Later versions make Aegisthus assist Clytemnestra or share responsibility for Agamemnon's death.
Aegisthus murders Cassandra’s infant sons upon their parents’ bodies.
Aegisthus removes her guardian bard and eventually overcomes her initial resistance.
Clytemnestra becomes Aegisthus’ partner and, in later traditions, bears his children.
They jointly murder Agamemnon and rule his household until Orestes returns.
Electra assists the plot that exposes Aegisthus to Orestes’ fatal attack.
Electra calls for Aegisthus’s death and insults his severed head after Orestes kills him.
Orestes returns and kills Agamemnon’s murderer and usurper.
The dominant genealogy makes Pelops Aegisthus’s ancestor through Thyestes.
Aegisthus belongs to the Tantalid line through Pelops and Thyestes.

Aegle.note: Aegle is Theseus’s lover in the Hesiodic account of Ariadne’s desertion.

Aegyptus.note: Aegyptus is Io’s descendant and father of the Danaids’ suitors.

Aelius.note: A Homeric scholion substitutes Aelius for Heleus among Andromeda’s sons.

Aerope.note: Later systematized genealogy names Aerope as his mother.
Aerope is named as Menelaus’ mother in tragedy and mythography.
Orestes is Aerope’s grandson through Agamemnon.

Aeson.note: Aeson is Jason’s essentially unanimous father.
Medea restores Aeson's youth by replacing his blood with a potion.

Aesop.note: Aesop accompanies Memnon in battle until Antilochus kills him.

Aesymnus.note: Hector kills Aesymnus during the Trojan War.

Aethalides.note: Aethalides serves the company as herald and negotiator, aided by unfailing memory.

Aethilla.note: Aethilla leads Trojan captives in burning the ships, forcing Protesilaus and his companions to settle.
