Aethiolas.note: A later genealogical variant names Aethiolas among Helen’s children.
A scholion lists Aethiolas among Menelaus’ variant sons.

Aethion.note: Scholastic tradition gives Aethion or Ethron as one of Laocoön’s sons.

Aethon.myth: Phaethon loses control of the solar horses
Aethon.note: Aethon bolts with the team when Phaethon cannot govern the chariot.

Aethra.note: Adrastus and the Argive mothers supplicate Aethra, who persuades Theseus to hear them.
The captured mother of Theseus becomes Helen’s attendant at Troy.
Aethra is Theseus’s mother and raises him at Troezen.

Aeëtes.note: Aeëtes imposes lethal trials on the company’s leader before refusing the promised Fleece.
After the Fleece is taken, Aeëtes and his forces pursue the escaping company.
Aeëtes orders Jason to complete lethal tasks before surrendering the fleece.
Jason removes Aeëtes’ fleece and flees while the Colchian king pursues him.
Medea is the daughter of Aeëtes in the standard genealogy.
Medea disobeys Aeëtes, helps Jason complete his trials, and flees.
Medea kills the usurping Perses and restores Aeëtes to power.

Agamedes.myth: Agamedes builds Amphitryon’s Theban bridal chamber
Agamedes.note: Regional tradition credits Agamedes and Trophonius with constructing the couple’s chamber.
Agamedes is Trophonius’ brother and fellow master-builder.
They appear together as labelled figures with Eunoos.
The brothers jointly place the stone threshold of Apollo’s temple.
The brothers participate together in a fragmentary Elean building narrative.
They request Apollo’s best human gift and die together.
Trophonius decapitates trapped Agamedes to prevent their identification.
Late notices make Agamedes Trophonius’ father rather than brother.
A varying late arrangement makes Agamedes Trophonius’ stepfather.

Aganus.note: Late genealogies make Aganus a child of Paris and Helen.

Agathe Tyche.note: Trophonius’ consultants lodge in a building shared with Agathe Tyche.

Agathon.note: Agathon is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Agathos Daimon.note: Trophonius’ consultants lodge in a building sacred to Agathos Daimon.

Agave.note: Agave, mother of Pentheus, is Cadmus’s daughter.
Cadmus questions Agave, restores her awareness, and laments the ruined family.
Under Dionysian madness, Agave leads the attack and tears apart her unrecognized son.

Agave.myth: Agave mistakes Pentheus for a boar
Agave.note: Agave calls Pentheus a boar, strikes first, and tears away his arm.
Agave is Semele’s sister in the Cadmean genealogy.
Agave falsely claims Semele conceived by a mortal and lied about Zeus.

Agelaus.note: Hector kills Agelaus during the Trojan War.
The herdsman Agelaus finds and raises the exposed infant Paris.

Agenor.note: Agenor is Cadmus’s father in the canonical Agenorid genealogy.
Agenor orders Cadmus to recover Europa and forbids returning without her.
Some genealogies insert Agenor differently within Io’s descendant line.
In a variant, Perseus defeats Agenor, Andromeda’s rival claimant.

Agriope.note: Agriope is Orpheus’s wife in a competing Hellenistic tradition.
Orpheus descends to Hades and persuades its rulers on Agriope’s behalf.

Agrius.note: Later genealogy names Agrius as Odysseus' son by Circe.

Aiacos of Garuda.note: Modern media reinvents Aeacus as the armored Specter Aiacos of Garuda.

Aidos.note: Icarius dedicates Aidos’s image after Penelope silently veils herself.

Ainippa.note: The departure krater labels Ainippa as Amphiaraus’ daughter or female family member.

Aiton.note: Learned genealogical tradition preserves Aiton as a variant parent.

Ajax son of Oileus.note: Ajax commands a contingent within Agamemnon's coalition.
Return traditions associate Agamemnon with a quarrel concerning Athena's wrath against Ajax.
The two Ajaxes fight together defending the wall and Patroclus’s body.
Ajax forcibly drags Cassandra from Athena’s image during Troy’s sack.
Later literary and visual traditions explicitly depict Ajax raping Cassandra.
Ajax and Nestor appear among the Achaean commanders and return traditions.
Ajax watches Palamedes and Thersites gaming in Polygnotus’s Delphi painting.

Ajax son of Telamon.note: Ajax serves under Agamemnon and joins the embassy seeking Achilles' return.
Diomedes fights Ajax in armed competition until spectators fear for Ajax’s life.
Helen identifies Ajax to Priam from Troy’s wall.
Nestor proposes the lottery in which Ajax is selected to face Hector.
Nestor devises an intelligence test helping decide between Ajax and Odysseus.
Priam asks Helen to identify Ajax among the Greek leaders.

Ajax the Great.note: Her spear strikes Ajax's greave but fails to penetrate it.

Ajax the Greater.note: Odysseus wrestles Ajax to an inconclusive result.
Odysseus defeats Ajax in the contest for Achilles' armor.
Ajax's shade refuses reconciliation because Odysseus won the armor.
Despite former enmity, Odysseus argues that Ajax deserves burial.

Ajax the Lesser.note: Odysseus reports or witnesses traditions concerning Ajax's sacrilege and death.

Ajax, son of Telamon.note: Ajax opposes Sarpedon's attack and kills his companion Epicles.

Alalcomeneus.note: Late commentary names Alalcomeneus as an alternative husband of Niobe.

Alcaeus.note: Amphitryon is Alcaeus’ son in the standard Perseid genealogy.
Alcaeus is a son of Andromeda and Perseus.
Alcaeus is listed among the sons of Perseus and Andromeda.

Alcathous.note: Alcathous is Pelops’s son in the Megarian genealogy.

Alcibie.note: Alcibie accompanies Penthesilea and is killed by Diomedes.

Alcimede.note: Pherecydes and Apollonius name Alcimede, daughter of Phylacus, as Jason’s mother.

Alcimedon.note: Alcimedon commands under Patroclus and later joins the fight over his corpse.

Alcinous.note: Alcinous judges whether the company must surrender Medea to the pursuing Colchians.
Alcinous shelters Jason and Medea while Colchian envoys demand Medea’s return.
Alcinous judges whether Medea must be returned to the Colchians.
Alcinous hosts Odysseus, hears his story, and sends him home.
Alcinous recalls the Phaeacians transporting Rhadamanthus to Tityus.

Alcmaeon.note: Alcmaeon is a son of Amphiaraus and Eriphyle.
Amphiaraus charges Alcmaeon to avenge him and attack Thebes.
Diomedes campaigns beside Alcmaeon, commander of the victorious Epigoni.
Diomedes and Alcmaeon jointly attack the usurpers who expelled Oeneus.

Alcmaon son of Thestor.note: Sarpedon kills Alcmaon while attacking the Achaean defenses.

Alcmena.note: Asius alone names Alcmena as a daughter of Amphiaraus.
Andromeda is an ancestress of Alcmena through Electryon.
Tiresias tells Alcmena her infant son’s heroic future.

Aletes.note: Some late accounts make Aletes the child of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus.
Electra’s return after false news helps precipitate Aletes’ overthrow and death.
Orestes kills Aegisthus’ son Aletes while recovering Mycenae.

Almus.note: Almus is named as a son of Sisyphus.

Alpheus.note: Heracles diverts the river Alpheus through Augeas’ cattle-yard.

Althaea.note: Althaea is Deianira’s mother in both principal genealogies.
Althaea is Leda’s sister in the Aetolian genealogy.
Althaea is Meleager's mother in the ordinary genealogy.
After he kills her brothers, Althaea invokes underworld powers against Meleager.
Althaea burns the billet bound to Meleager's life, causing his death.

Amazons.note: Bellerophon attacks and kills the Amazon army; no individual is named.
Priam recalls being present when the Amazons attacked his Phrygian allies.

Ameinias.note: Narcissus rejects Ameinias and sends him the sword used for suicide.
Dying at Narcissus' door, Ameinias invokes divine vengeance against him.

Amenhotep III.note: Greek and Roman visitors identified Amenhotep III’s Theban colossus as Memnon.

Ammon.note: Ammon’s oracle declares that Andromeda must be exposed to save the country.

Amphilochus.note: Amphilochus is a son of Amphiaraus and Eriphyle.
Amphilochus and Diomedes are fellow members of the Epigoni.
Amphilochus is named among the participants or witnesses at Polyxena’s sacrifice.
One inconsistent genealogy makes Amphilochus Tiresias’s descendant through Manto.

Amphimedon.note: Odysseus' party kills Amphimedon in the palace battle.
Amphimedon wounds Telemachus in the wrist during the battle.

Amphinome.note: A later genealogical variant names Amphinome as Jason’s mother.

Amphinomus.note: Odysseus obliquely warns the comparatively restrained suitor Amphinomus.
Amphinomus courts Penelope and is treated comparatively favorably by her household.
Telemachus kills Amphinomus with a spear as he rushes Odysseus.

Amphion.note: Nestor descends from Amphion through Amphion’s daughter Chloris.
Amphion is Niobe's husband and father of her children.
Amphion is Tantalus’s son-in-law through his marriage to Niobe.

Amphithea.note: Amphithea, daughter of Pronax, is Adrastus's wife.

Amyclas.note: Amyclas survives as Niobe's son in Telesilla's version.

Amycus.note: The hostile king challenges the company and is defeated or killed by Polydeuces.
Amycus opposes Jason’s company but is personally defeated by Polydeuces.

Anaphe.note: Anaphe is a child of Minos in regional genealogy.

Anaxibia.note: Hyginus names Anaxibia, daughter of Bias, as Alcestis’ mother.
Later genealogical variants name Anaxibia or Astynome as Menelaus’ sister.
A Hesiodic and mythographic tradition names Anaxibia as Nestor’s wife.
Eustathius harmonizes the variants by making Anaxibia Nestor’s second wife.

Anaxo.note: Pseudo-Apollodorus names Anaxo as Alcmene’s mother.

Ancaeus.note: Ancaeus succeeds Tiphys as helmsman and navigates for the company.
Ancaeus hunts beside Atalanta before the boar kills him.

Ancaeus of Arcadia.note: Ancaeus joins Meleager's hunt and is killed by the boar.

Anchialus.note: Hector kills Anchialus during the Trojan War.

Anchises.note: Cassandra’s migration prophecy is recalled within Anchises and Aeneas’s family narrative.

Anchises.myth: Anchises orders withdrawal after Laocoön’s omen
Anchises.note: Anchises interprets Laocoön’s household omen and orders Aeneas to leave Troy.
Dares includes the collateral Trojan kinsman Anchises in Priam's council.

Anchurus.note: Midas' son Anchurus sacrifices himself to close the destructive chasm.

Androgeos.note: Androgeos’s death prompts Minos to impose the Athenian tribute Theseus confronts.

Androgeus.note: Androgeus is Minos’s son, whose death precipitates war with Athens.

Antaeus.note: Heracles lifts Antaeus away from Earth and kills him while wrestling.

Antandre.note: Antandre accompanies Penthesilea and is killed by Achilles.

Antenor.myth: Antenor helps Amphitryon ignite Alcmene’s pyre
Antenor.note: Antenor assists Amphitryon in bringing fire against Alcmene in the pyre scene.
Helen recalls Antenor hosting the embassy of Odysseus and Menelaus.
Tzetzes preserves the alternative genealogy making Laocoön Antenor’s son.
Antenor hosts or recalls Menelaus’ embassy and describes his concise speech.
Antenor receives Odysseus' embassy and is later protected during the sack.
Antenor supports restitution, which Paris refuses in later accounts.
Antenor stands beside Priam as Trojan elder during the wall and oath scenes.
Dares makes Antenor Priam's envoy and counselor in policy against Greece.

Antibrote.note: Antibrote accompanies Penthesilea and is killed by Achilles.

Anticleia.note: Mother of Odysseus in Homeric genealogy.
He attempts three times to embrace her shade in Hades.
Sisyphus impregnates Anticleia before her marriage; her consent is textually unclear.

Anticlus.note: Odysseus restrains Anticlus from answering Helen's imitated voice.
Later elaboration says Odysseus suffocates Anticlus while silencing him.

Antilochus.note: Antilochus’ death at Memnon’s hands prompts Achilles’ revenge.
Some traditions place Antilochus’ ashes with Achilles and Patroclus.
Ajax directs Antilochus to report Patroclus’s death to Achilles.
Ajax and Antilochus participate as athletic competitors.
Memnon kills Antilochus after the hero intervenes to save Nestor.
Antilochus blocks Menelaus dangerously, then apologizes and receives forgiveness.
Antilochus is Nestor’s son and Trojan companion.
Antilochus saves his endangered father from Memnon and dies doing so.
Antilochus tells Achilles of Patroclus’ death and restrains his hands.
Antilochus appears near Protesilaus in Polygnotus's depiction of Hades.

Antimachus.note: Bribed by Paris, Antimachus urges the Trojans to kill Menelaus and Odysseus.

Antinous.note: Odysseus shoots Antinous first during the palace slaughter.
Penelope delays Antinous and the other suitors by secretly unweaving Laertes’s shroud.
Penelope rebukes Antinous for plotting to kill Telemachus.
A later variant says Antinous seduces Penelope, prompting her dismissal.
Antinous insults Telemachus and organizes an ambush intended to kill him.

Antion.note: Diodorus names Antion as Ixion’s father.

Antiope.note: A variant genealogy names Antiope rather than Hippolyte as his mother.
Servian and Euphorionic tradition names Antiope as Laocoön’s wife and sexual partner.
Learned genealogical consolidation sometimes includes Antiope among her sisters.
Antiope is Theseus’s Amazon partner and mother of Hippolytus.
Theseus abducts Antiope after sailing independently against the Amazons.
In one tradition Heracles awards Antiope to Theseus as a prize.
An epic variant says Antiope voluntarily boards Theseus’s ship from love.
Antiope attacks during Theseus’s wedding to Phaedra in one tradition.
Some accounts make Theseus himself kill Antiope during the Amazon conflict.

Antiphates.note: Antiphates is Amphiaraus’ grandfather through Oicles.
Hyginus names Antiphates as one of Laocoön’s sons.
Laocoön attempts unsuccessfully to save Antiphates during the serpent attack.
Antiphates is named among the participants or witnesses at Polyxena’s sacrifice.

Antiphus.note: Apollodorus lists Antiphus among Hecuba's sons.
Antiphus is listed among Priam's sons by Hecuba.

Antitheus.note: Penthesilea kills Antitheus during her battlefield rampage.

Aones.note: Cadmus confronts the Aones, permitting some inhabitants to remain.

Apollo Cillaeus.note: Pelops establishes a sanctuary for Apollo Cillaeus after burying Cillus.

Apollo Paean.note: Apollo Paean receives worship on Amphiaraus’ divided altar at Oropos.

Apollo at Delphi.note: Apollo's oracle orders Actaeon's burial and a bound bronze image.

Apsyrtus.note: Jason kills the adult pursuer after Medea lures him to a sanctuary meeting.
Medea kills and dismembers the child, delaying Aeëtes while the company escapes.

Apsyrtus.myth: Ambush during the flight from Colchis
Apsyrtus.note: Jason ambushes and kills the adult Apsyrtus, then mutilates his corpse with Medea.
Apsyrtus is Medea's brother in several conflicting traditions.
Medea kills and dismembers her child brother to delay Aeëtes.
Medea lures her adult brother to a meeting where Jason ambushes him.

Arcas.note: Callisto bears Arcas, the Arcadian culture hero and son of Zeus.
Unaware of her identity, Arcas prepares to spear Callisto before Jupiter intervenes.

Arcesius.note: Odysseus is Arcesius' grandson through Laertes.

Archemachus.note: Archemachus is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Areius.note: Neoptolemus is ancestor of Pergamus, who defeats Areius and becomes an eponym.

Arete.note: Arete warns Jason and Medea, enabling marriage and preventing Medea’s extradition.
Arete arranges Jason’s marriage to Medea before Aeëtes’ envoys can reclaim her.
Arete protects Medea and secretly arranges her immediate marriage to Jason.
Odysseus supplicates Arete, who questions and assists him.

Aretus.note: Aretus is one of Nestor’s sons present at Pylos.
Aretus is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Argia.note: Argia, wife of Polynices, is Adrastus's daughter.
Adrastus gives Argia in marriage to the exiled Polynices.
Polynices' wife joins Antigone in recovering and cremating his body.
Argia is named as Io’s mother alongside Inachus.

Argus.note: Argus builds Argo under Athena’s direction and joins the crew.

Argus.myth: Construction and voyage of the Argo
Argus.note: Argus builds the Argo and sails as a member of Jason’s expedition.
Argus is Medea's nephew through her sister Chalciope.
The rescue of Argus helps connect Medea with Jason.

Aricie.note: Racine gives Hippolytus a legitimate beloved named Aricie.

Arion.myth: Adrastus escapes the failed Theban expedition
Arion.note: Adrastus alone escapes from Thebes on his divine, exceptionally swift horse.

Arisbe.note: Arisbe is Priam's first wife and the mother of Aesacus.

Aristaeus.note: Aristaeus is Actaeon's father in the standard Theban genealogy.

Aristaeus.myth: Recovery and burial of Actaeon's remains
Aristaeus.note: Actaeon's ghost directs Aristaeus to recover and bury his cervine remains.
Aristaeus’s pursuit causes Eurydice’s fatal flight and initiates Orpheus’s tragedy.

Aristodeme.note: Aristodeme is listed among Priam's daughters by other women.

Aristomachus.note: Aristomachus is Adrastus's brother in Pseudo-Apollodorus's genealogy.

Aristomenes.note: Aristomenes dedicates his recovered shield in Trophonius’ sanctuary.
Trophonius orders Aristomenes’ shield displayed before battle.

Arne.note: A later genealogical variant names Arne as Jason’s mother.

Arsinoe.note: The nurse Arsinoe saves Orestes from Clytemnestra.

Asaeus.note: Hector kills Asaeus during the Trojan War.

Asius.note: Homer identifies Asius, son of Dymas, as Hecuba's brother.

Asopus.note: Aeacus is Asopus’s grandson through Aegina.
Sisyphus trades information about Aegina's abductor for water at Corinth.

Assaon.note: In the Parthenius variant, Niobe is Assaon's daughter.
Assaon desires Niobe incestuously, but she refuses him.
After Niobe rejects him, Assaon burns her children to death.

Asterion.note: Asterion raises Minos as his foster-son and precedes him as king.

Asterius.note: Asterius marries Europa and raises Sarpedon with her other sons.

Asterodia.note: Asterodia is Penelope’s mother in a scholastic genealogy.

Asteropeus.note: Asteropeus wounds Achilles during their fight beside the river.
Achilles kills Asteropeus after being wounded by him.

Astyanax.note: Andromache and Hector are the parents of Astyanax, also called Scamandrius.
Andromache mourns as the Greeks take her son away to die.
Racine’s Andromaque protects her surviving son from Greek dynastic vengeance.
Astyanax, Hector's son, is Hecuba's grandson.
Hecuba receives and prepares his corpse for burial on Hector's shield.
Neoptolemus snatches Astyanax from his nurse and throws him from a tower.

Astyanax.myth: Polyxena and Astyanax condemned after Troy
Astyanax.note: Seneca structurally pairs Polyxena and Astyanax as victims of Greek victory.
Astyanax is Priam's grandson through Hector.
Archaic vase painters show Neoptolemus striking Priam with Astyanax's corpse.

Astydameia.note: One mythographic genealogy names Astydameia as Amphitryon’s mother.
Astydameia is a daughter of Pelops in later genealogical traditions.

Astydamia.note: Acastus’ wife desires Peleus and attempts to seduce him, but he refuses.
After rejection, she falsely accuses Peleus of attempting rape or seduction.
Peleus kills Acastus’ wife after capturing Iolcus; scholia add dismemberment.

Astygonus.note: Astygonus is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Astymedusa.note: Astymedusa appears as an additional wife in later scholastic genealogies.

Astyoche.note: Later genealogical systematization lists Astyoche among Priam's siblings.

Atas.note: Atas is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Athamas.note: Athamas is Sisyphus's brother in Aeolid genealogy.

Athena Paeonia.note: Athena Paeonia receives worship on Amphiaraus’ divided altar at Oropos.

Atreus.note: Homer names Atreus as Agamemnon's father.
A variant makes Atreus his grandfather and foster-father.
Agamemnon inherits kingship and the divine sceptre through Atreus.
The dominant Homeric genealogy makes Menelaus a son of Atreus.
Orestes is Atreus’ grandson through Agamemnon.
Atreus is a recurrent son of Pelops and Hippodamia.
Pelops transmits Zeus’s royal sceptre to Atreus.
Pelops curses and exiles Atreus for involvement in Chrysippus’s murder.
Atreus is Tantalus’s grandson through Pelops.

Atreus.myth: Atreus repeats the ancestral cannibal feast
Atreus.note: Tantalus’s compelled ghost instigates Atreus’s feast of Thyestes’s sons.

Atymnius.note: Atymnius replaces Miletus as the youth contested by Minos and Sarpedon.
Atymnius replaces Miletus as Sarpedon's preferred beloved in a reported variant.

Augeas.note: Trophonius and Agamedes are associated with building Augeas’ treasury.
Later scholia explain the Elean association as the treasury’s robbery.

Auson.note: A later genealogy makes Auson his son by Calypso.

Autochthe.note: Some later genealogical lists add Autochthe among Andromeda’s children.

Autolycus.note: Autolycus names Odysseus and hosts the hunt producing his scar.
Autolycus steals Sisyphus's cattle, but Sisyphus marks or tracks them and proves ownership.

Automedon.note: Hector attempts to capture Achilles' immortal horses from Automedon.
Automedon drives Achilles’ immortal horses for Patroclus and fights beside him.

Autonoe.note: Autonoe is Actaeon's mother in the standard Theban genealogy.
Autonoe mourns and searches for her son's unrecognized cervine remains.
Autonoe, mother of Actaeon, is Cadmus’s daughter.
The maddened Autonoe joins the maenads in dismembering Pentheus.
Autonoe first discovers Pentheus and later tears away one of his shoulders.
Autonoe is Semele’s sister in the Cadmean genealogy.
Autonoe joins the false accusation that Semele lied about Zeus.

Autonous.note: Hector kills Autonous during the Trojan War.
Patroclus kills Autonous during his final assault toward Troy.

Aëdon.note: Aëdon is the nightingale child-killer analogous to or treated as an alternate Procne.

Baton.note: Baton is Amphiaraus’ charioteer and companion, usually swallowed with him.

Belleros.note: Learned tradition makes Bellerophon kill Belleros, explaining the hero’s name.

Belus.note: Belus descends from Io through the Egyptian genealogical line.

Bias.note: Bias is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Bouldy.note: The game depicts an affectionate relationship between Sisyphus and his personified boulder.

Bremusa.note: Bremusa accompanies Penthesilea and is killed by Idomeneus.

Briseis.note: Briseis is awarded to Achilles, seized by Agamemnon, and later restored.
Agamemnon seizes the enslaved Briseis as compensation for returning Chryseis.
Agamemnon restores Briseis to Achilles and swears he did not violate her.
Patroclus receives Briseis and later promises to arrange her marriage to Achilles.

Britomartis.note: Minos pursues Britomartis for nine months until she escapes into the sea.

Broteas.note: Broteas is Niobe's brother in some Tantalid genealogies.
Broteas is Pelops’s brother in later Tantalid genealogies.
Broteas is named as Tantalus’s son.

Bubo.note: The mechanical owl Bubo assists Perseus in the modern film adaptation.

Bucolion.note: Later genealogical systematization lists Bucolion among Priam's siblings.

Bunomus.note: Late genealogies make Bunomus a child of Paris and Helen.

Busiris.note: A possibly distinct Pygmalion is identified as Busiris’ brother.

Butes.note: Butes deserts the ship for the Sirens but is rescued by Aphrodite.
Orpheus fails to restrain fellow Argonaut Butes, who leaps toward the Sirens.
Butes is the brother of Philomela and Procne.

Byblus’ queen.myth: Io recovers Epaphus from Byblus’ queen
Byblus’ queen.note: The queen raises stolen Epaphus until Io finds and recovers him.

Cacus.note: Hercules kills Cacus after the monster steals cattle from Geryon’s herd.

Caeneus.note: Nestor recalls Caeneus as his comrade against the Centaurs.
Caeneus and Theseus fight together against the Centaurs.

Calais.note: Calais serves in the company and pursues the Harpies with Zetes.
Calais accompanies Jason and helps drive the Harpies away from Phineus.
Calais and Orpheus serve together among the Argonauts.
Orpheus loves Calais and consequently introduces male love to Thrace.

Calchas.note: Calchas reveals that Agamemnon's treatment of Chryses caused Apollo's plague.
Calchas declares that Iphigenia must be sacrificed after Agamemnon's offense.
Calchas explains Athena’s anger and warns that the day threatens Ajax.
Calchas declares that Andromache’s son must die before the Greeks can sail.
Calchas declares that Artemis requires Iphigenia’s sacrifice before the fleet can sail.
Calchas’ prophetic or ritual counsel helps define Troy’s fall and post-sack sacrifices.
Calchas announces that the Greeks must fetch Philoctetes.
Calchas interprets and authorizes the supernatural demand requiring Polyxena’s death.

Calibos.note: The film invents Calibos as an antagonist confronted by Perseus.

Callidice.note: Odysseus marries the Thesprotian queen Callidice.
Odysseus shares Callidice's rule and war before returning after her death.

Calliope.note: Calliope is Orpheus’s mother in the dominant later genealogy.
Calliope joins the Muses in gathering or mourning Orpheus’s remains.

Callithyia.note: Genealogical systematizers sometimes merge Io with Hera’s first Argive priestess.

Candybus.note: A late Lycian tradition sometimes calls the local eponym Deucalion's son.

Canthus.note: Canthus sails with the company until Caphaurus kills him in Libya.

Capaneus.note: Capaneus serves among Adrastus's champions in the war against Thebes.

Capaneus.myth: Funeral oration for the fallen champions
Capaneus.note: Adrastus praises Capaneus's character after the recovery of the bodies.
Capaneus and Amphiaraus serve together among the Seven against Thebes.

Cassiopeia.note: Her offensive comparison with the Nereids causes the punishment imposed upon Andromeda.
Perseus becomes Cassiopeia’s son-in-law after rescuing Andromeda.

Cassiphone.note: Later genealogy names Cassiphone as Odysseus' child by Circe.
Cassiphone is Telemachus’ paternal half-sister, daughter of Odysseus and Circe.
The resurrected Odysseus gives Cassiphone to Telemachus as his wife.
Cassiphone kills Telemachus after he kills her mother Circe.

Castianeira.note: Castianeira of Aesyme is Priam's wife and Gorgythion's mother.

Catreus.note: Catreus is Minos’s son and successor.

Cayster.note: A late Ephesian genealogy makes the river Cayster her son.

Cebren.note: The river-god Cebren is Oenone's father and Paris's father-in-law.

Cebriones.note: Cebriones is Hector's half-brother and charioteer.
Cebriones serves as Hector's charioteer until Patroclus kills him.
Patroclus kills Hector’s charioteer Cebriones with a stone.
Cebriones is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Centaurs.note: Pindar makes Ixion their ancestor through Centaurus and the Magnesian mares.
Later mythographers make Ixion and the Cloud direct parents of the Centaurs.

Centaurus.myth: Birth of Centaurus from the cloud-image
Centaurus.note: Ixion and the cloud-image produce Centaurus, progenitor of the horse-Centaurs.

Cephalus.myth: Cephalus joins the fox hunt and Taphian war
Cephalus.note: Amphitryon recruits Cephalus, Laelaps’ owner, for both the fox crisis and expedition.
Aeacus receives Cephalus and promises Myrmidon troops to Athens.

Cepheus.note: He exposes Andromeda under pressure and promises her to Perseus for rescuing her.
Cepheus appears with Meleager among the assembled hunters.
Cepheus promises Andromeda to Perseus in return for her rescue.

Cephisus.note: Cephisus receives worship on Amphiaraus’ divided altar at Oropos.
Cephisus fathers Narcissus after raping Liriope.

Cercyon.note: Theseus defeats the murderous Cercyon in wrestling.

Ceroessa.note: A Constantinopolitan local legend makes Ceroessa another child of Io.

Ceryneian hind.note: Heracles pursues and captures Artemis’ sacred hind without killing it.

Cestrinus.note: Pausanias names Cestrinus as Andromache’s son by Helenus.

Ceteus.note: Pherecydes’ alternative genealogy makes Callisto the daughter of Ceteus.
A scholion names Ceteus as Callisto’s father and Stilbe as her mother.

Cetus.note: Perseus kills the sea creature, aided by Andromeda in early art.

Ceyx.note: Ceyx receives and shelters the blood-guilty Peleus at Trachis.

Chalciope.note: Chalciope uses her sons’ rescue to help obtain Medea’s aid for the company.
Their interests converge because Chalciope's sons support Jason.

Chariclo.note: Later tradition sometimes makes Chiron’s wife Achilles’ foster-mother.
Athena tells Chariclo that Autonoe would prefer Actaeon blind rather than dead.
Chariclo participates in the household that fosters Jason.
Chariclo appears in a tradition concerning Peleus’ maternal ancestry.
Chariclo, Athena’s nymph companion, is Tiresias’s mother.
Chariclo protests his blindness and obtains compensatory gifts from Athena.

Chelidon.note: Chelidon is Aëdon's swallow-named sister and the regional analogue of Philomela.

Chersidamas.note: Chersidamas is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Chloris.note: Chloris, daughter of Amphion, is Nestor’s mother.
Chloris, also called Meliboea, survives as Niobe's daughter in several variants.

Chorea.note: Perseus kills the Dionysian follower Chorea during his Argive victory.

Christ.note: Christian funerary art uses Orpheus as a typological image of Christ bringing harmony and salvation.

Chromius.note: Chromius and Nestor are sons of Neleus and Chloris.
Chromius is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Chrysaor.note: Chrysaor springs from Medusa’s severed neck when Perseus strikes.

Chryse.note: Later accounts associate the nymph or sacred power Chryse with the serpent attack.

Chryseis.note: The dispute over Chryseis indirectly precipitates Achilles’ quarrel with Agamemnon.
Agamemnon claims Chryseis as a captive and threatens sexual exploitation.
Divine compulsion forces Agamemnon to return her without ransom.

Chryses.note: Agamemnon insults Apollo's priest and refuses his ransom.
Agamemnon ultimately returns Chryses' daughter under divine pressure.
He is her paternal half-brother through Agamemnon and Chryseis.
After recognizing their kinship, he helps Iphigenia and kills Thoas.
Chryses is attributed to Minos by later genealogical traditions.

Chrysippus.note: Chrysippus is Pelops’s favored son by varying mothers.

Chrysothemis.note: Chrysothemis is consistently named among Agamemnon's daughters.

Chthonius.note: Chthonius survives the Spartoi conflict and becomes a Theban ancestor.

Cilissa.note: His former nurse mourns the false death report and summons Aegisthus.

Cilix.note: Cilix is Cadmus’s brother and fellow searcher for Europa.

Cilla.note: Later genealogical systematization lists Cilla among Priam's siblings.

Cillus.note: Cillus serves as Pelops’s charioteer before dying on Lesbos.

Cinyras.note: Cinyras becomes Pygmalion’s son-in-law by marrying Metharme.

Cisseus.note: Euripides gives Cisseus as Hecuba's father.

Cleanto.note: Cleanto is added as Cadmus’s daughter in some late genealogies.

Cleola.note: A fragmentary genealogical variant names Cleola as his mother.

Cleolla.note: One Hesiodic arrangement makes Cleolla the mother of Menelaus.

Cleopatra.note: The chorus invokes Cleopatra's family tragedy as an analogue for Antigone.

Clete.note: Her nurse or attendant sails searching for her and reaches southern Italy.

Clonie.note: Clonie accompanies Penthesilea, whose death provokes her queen's retaliation.

Clonius.note: Clonius is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Closter.note: Pliny names the spindle-inventor Closter as Arachne's son.

Clymene.note: Later genealogical traditions alternatively name Clymene as Admetus’ mother.

Clymenus.note: Hyginus' alternative genealogy makes Clymenus, son of Sol, Phaethon's father.

Clysonymus.note: Patroclus unintentionally kills Amphidamas’ son, later named Clysonymus, during a quarrel.

Clytia.note: Hyginus gives Clytia, rather than Idyia, as Medea's mother.

Clytie.note: Another scholiastic genealogy names Clytie or Clytia as Pelops’s mother.

Clytius.note: Later genealogical systematization lists Clytius among Priam's siblings.

Cocalus.note: Cocalus receives Minos as a guest while secretly protecting Daedalus.

Colchian dragon.note: The Fleece’s guardian is drugged, enchanted or otherwise overcome for the company.

Coon.note: Coon wounds Agamemnon while defending his brother Iphidamas' body.

Copreus.note: Copreus appears among Pelops’s sons in later genealogical lists.

Coroebus.note: Coroebus comes as Cassandra’s suitor and defender but dies during Troy’s sack.

Corythus.note: Corythus is usually Paris's son by Oenone.

Cres.note: A divergent genealogy makes Rhadamanthus a descendant of Cres.

Crete.note: Crete appears as an alternative wife of Minos.

Cretheus.note: Cretheus is normally Jason’s paternal grandfather.

Creusa.note: Creusa is included among Cassandra’s Trojan sisters.

Ctesippus.note: Ctesippus is Deianira’s son by Heracles.

Ctimene.note: Ctimene is Odysseus' sister in the Homeric family.

Curetes.note: At Hera’s command, the Curetes abduct Io’s newborn son.

Cyanippus.note: Cyanippus is Adrastus's son in a late genealogy.

Cynurus.note: Later genealogical lists add Cynurus among Andromeda’s children.

Damocrateia.note: Damocrateia is named as Aeacus’s daughter in later genealogy.

Danaids.note: The Danaids invoke Io as their Argive ancestress.

Danaus.note: Danaus descends from Io and returns from Egypt to Argos.

Deidameia.note: Post-Homeric tradition names Deidameia as Neoptolemus’ mother.

Deidamia.note: Achilles impregnates Deidamia while concealed among Lycomedes’ daughters.

Deino.note: Perseus compels Deino with her sisters by withholding their shared eye.

Deiochus.note: Paris kills Deiochus from behind while he flees.

Deiopites.note: Deiopites is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Democoon.note: Democoon is Priam's son and is killed during the Iliadic fighting.

Dia.note: Dia is Ixion’s wife in Homer and the later genealogy.

Dias.note: Dias appears among Pelops’s sons in later genealogical lists.

Dictys.note: Dictys hauls Danaë and infant Perseus ashore in his net.

Eilissus.note: Penthesilea kills Eilissus during her battlefield rampage.

Elasippus.note: Penthesilea kills Elasippus during her battlefield rampage.

Ephesus.note: A late genealogy makes Ephesus her grandson through Cayster.

Eryx.note: Heracles wrestles and kills Eryx during the cattle journey.
