Helenus is Hecuba's son in epic and mythographic genealogy.
Menelaus wounds Helenus through his bow hand.
Helenus’ prophecy reveals that Troy requires Achilles’ son.
Helenus later serves Neoptolemus as captive and adviser.
Neoptolemus gives Helenus Andromache and, in some accounts, part of his realm.
Odysseus captures or induces Helenus to reveal how Troy can fall.
Helenus prophesies disaster and warns Paris against sailing to Sparta.
Peleus receives Thetis’ instruction that Andromache is to marry Helenus.
Helenus’ prophecy reveals that Philoctetes is necessary for Troy’s capture.
Helenus is Priam's son and a Trojan seer.

Helenus son of Oenops.note: Hector kills Helenus son of Oenops during the Trojan War.

Heleus.note: Heleus serves as one of Amphitryon’s allies in the campaign.
Heleus is a son of Andromeda in the Apollodoran genealogy.
Heleus is listed among the sons of Perseus and Andromeda.

Heliades.note: The Heliades are Phaethon's sisters in the principal accounts.

Heliades.myth: The Heliades yoke the solar horses
Heliades.note: Some variants blame Phaethon's sisters for yoking the horses before his ride.

Hera Heniochos.note: Consultants sacrifice to Hera Heniochos before consulting Trophonius.

Hercle.note: Etruscan tradition adapts Heracles as the divine figure Hercle.

Hercyna.note: The local river nymph’s waters and images are associated with Trophonius’ cult.

Hermione.note: Hermione accuses Andromache of sorcery and plots to kill her and Molossus.
Electra participates in the scheme that seizes Hermione and threatens her life.
Hermione is Helen’s daughter by Menelaus.
Helen prepares a woven robe for Hermione’s future marriage.
Hermione is the daughter of Menelaus and Helen.
Menelaus promises Hermione to Neoptolemus and later protects her against Andromache.
Menelaus promises Hermione to Neoptolemus and celebrates their marriage.
Later tradition depicts Neoptolemus forcibly appropriating Hermione from Orestes.
Hermione is Orestes’ disputed first and ultimately assigned wife.
Orestes seizes Hermione as a hostage during his attack on Helen.
Peleus thwarts Hermione’s faction when it attempts to kill Andromache and Molossus.
Hermione is a descendant of Tantalus through Pelops, Atreus, and Menelaus.

Hermodice.note: Hermodice, called Demodice by Pollux, is named as Midas' wife.

Hesione.note: Acusilaus's genealogy makes Oceanus's daughter Hesione Deucalion's mother.
Heracles saves Hesione from a sea monster before Laomedon withholds payment.
The pseudo-Hesiodic Aegimius names Hesione as Palamedes’s mother.
Hesione is Priam's sister in the developed genealogy.
Hesione chooses and redeems captive Podarces, who is subsequently called Priam.

Hesperian Naiads.note: The Hesperian Naiads bury Phaethon's smouldering body and inscribe his epitaph.

Hesperides.note: The Hesperides direct the exhausted company to water after Heracles’ passage.
The Hesperides raise Memnon beside Ocean during his childhood.

Hicetaon.note: Later genealogical systematization lists Hicetaon among Priam's siblings.

Hippalcimus.note: Hippalcimus appears among Pelops’s sons in later genealogical lists.

Hippalmus.note: Penthesilea tramples Hippalmus beneath her horse.

Hippasus.note: Hippasus appears among Pelops’s sons in later genealogical lists.

Hippodamas.note: Hippodamas is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Hippodameia.note: Orestes descends from Hippodameia through Atreus and Agamemnon.

Hippodamia.note: Pelops wins and marries Hippodamia, mother of many Pelopids.
Hippodamia desires Pelops and recruits Myrtilus to secure his victory.
Pelops becomes angry with Hippodamia, who withdraws to Midea.
Her supposed marriage supplies the pretext for Polydectes’ gift demand.
A Christian-era variant names Hippodamia as Sarpedon's mother.

Hippolochus.note: Hippolochus is Bellerophon’s son and continues the Lycian lineage.

Hippolyta.note: Hippolyta initially gives her belt willingly to Heracles.
After Hera provokes battle, Heracles kills Hippolyta in one influential version.
Learned genealogies make the Amazon queen Penthesilea's sister.
Penthesilea accidentally kills her sister while throwing at a stag.
A variant places Hippolyta's accidental death amid Theseus' wedding battle.

Hippolyte.note: Euripides names the Amazon Hippolyte as Hippolytus’ mother.
Hippolyte is an alternative Amazon wife or partner of Theseus.
Under this naming variant, Theseus captures or abducts Hippolyte.

Hippomedon.note: Hippomedon is one of Adrastus's champions against Thebes.

Hippomedon.myth: Funeral oration for the fallen champions
Hippomedon.note: Adrastus praises Hippomedon after the recovery of the Argive dead.
Hippomedon and Amphiaraus serve together among the Seven against Thebes.

Hippomenes.note: Hippomenes races and defeats Atalanta using Aphrodite’s golden apples.
Hippomenes becomes Atalanta’s husband after winning the race.
They commit sanctuary sacrilege and are transformed and yoked together as lions.

Hipponome.note: One mythographic genealogy names Hipponome as Amphitryon’s mother.

Hipponous.note: Hipponous is Adrastus's son in Hyginus's divergent account.
Hector kills Hipponous during the Trojan War.
Apollodorus lists Hipponous among Hecuba's sons.
Hipponous is listed among Priam's sons by Hecuba.

Hippothoe.note: Hippothoe accompanies Penthesilea and is killed by Achilles.

Hippothous.note: Ajax kills Hippothous while he drags Patroclus’s corpse.
Hippothous is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Historis.myth: Historis tricks Hera’s agents during Alcmene’s labor
Historis.note: Historis falsely announces the birth, causing the Pharmacides to release their obstruction.

Hyacinthus.note: Hyacinthus and Narcissus are jointly listed among the beautiful dead.

Hyantes.note: Cadmus defeats or expels the Hyantes during his establishment in Boeotia.

Hydra of Lerna.note: The Hydra’s venom contaminates Nessus’ blood and makes Deianira’s garment lethal.

Hygieia.note: Amphiaraus and Hygieia jointly issue a dream command concerning Moschos’ manumission.

Hylaeus.note: Atalanta fights Hylaeus when he attempts to rape her.
Atalanta shoots and kills the assaulting centaur Hylaeus.

Hylas.note: Hylas accompanies the expedition until a nymph abducts him and the ship leaves.
Theocritus portrays Hylas as Heracles’ beloved young companion.
Heracles abandons the Argonautic voyage to search for Hylas.
Hylas serves in Jason’s expedition but disappears in Mysia without a distinct exchange.

Hylas.myth: Water myths on the Ostia wellhead
Hylas.note: Hylas and Narcissus appear compositionally together without narrative interaction.

Hyllus.note: Alcmene is Hyllus’ grandmother through Heracles.

Hyllus.myth: Hyllus sends Eurystheus’ head to Alcmene
Hyllus.note: Hyllus delivers Eurystheus’ severed head, enabling Alcmene’s posthumous vengeance.
Hyllus is Deianira’s son by Heracles.
Hyllus accuses Deianira, discovers her body, and later learns she was deceived.

Hyperenor.note: Hyperenor survives the Spartoi conflict and becomes a Theban ancestor.

Hypermestra.note: Hypermestra is Io’s Danaid descendant whose marriage continues the Argive line.

Hypermnestra.note: Later genealogies name Hypermnestra as Amphiaraus’ mother.
Hypermnestra is Leda’s sister in the Aetolian genealogy.

Hypirochus.note: Hypirochus is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Hypsipyle.note: Hypsipyle guides Adrastus and his army to water, leaving Opheltes unattended.
Amphiaraus encounters Hypsipyle seeking water and interprets her charge’s death.
Hypsipyle receives the company; Jason and other crewmen form unions with Lemnian women.
Jason sleeps with Hypsipyle during the Argonauts’ stay on Lemnos.

Hypsipyle.myth: Hypsipyle guides the thirsty army to a spring
Hypsipyle.note: She leaves Opheltes temporarily and guides the Seven to water at Nemea.

Hyrieus.note: Hyrieus employs Trophonius and Agamedes to construct his treasure-house.
Trophonius repeatedly steals from Hyrieus through a removable building stone.
Trophonius defeats Hyrieus’ locks and seals using the hidden entrance.

Iasion.note: Iasion is Atalanta’s father in Aelian’s Arcadian version.

Iasus.note: Iasus is Atalanta’s father in an Arcadian genealogy.
Wanting a son, Iasus exposes the infant Atalanta.
Iasus is Io’s father in a competing Argive genealogy.

Idaeus.note: Late genealogies make Idaeus a child of Paris and Helen.
The herald Idaeus drives Priam's wagon and accompanies him to Achilles' shelter.

Idas.note: Idas sails with the company despite violent arguments and a challenge to Apollo.
Idas and Atalanta appear together in hunter or Argonaut catalogues.

Idas.myth: Debate over divine and magical aid
Idas.note: Idas challenges Jason’s reliance on divine or magical assistance.
Meleager and his father-in-law Idas later appear together as Argonauts.

Idmon.note: Idmon, a purple-dyer of Colophon, is Arachne's father.
Idmon reads omens for the company before dying from a boar wound.
Idmon serves as a seer under Jason and dies during the voyage.

Idomeneus.note: The Cretan commander serves in the coalition and receives Agamemnon's praise.
Ajax and Idomeneus serve together as Achaean commanders.
Ajax and Idomeneus participate in Patroclus’s games.
Hector exchanges threats and attacks with Idomeneus during the fighting.
Helen identifies Idomeneus and recalls him as Menelaus’s guest.
Minos is the grandfather and dynastic ancestor of Idomeneus.
Idomeneus joins the defense of Patroclus and the funeral community.
A son named Idomeneus appears in Apollodorus's Priamid catalog.
Priam asks Helen to identify the Greek commander Idomeneus.
Telemachus and Mentor help reform Idomeneus’ government in Fénelon’s narrative.

Idyia.note: Idyia is Medea's mother in the standard early genealogy.

Iliona.note: Later catalogues add Iliona among Hecuba's children.

Illyrius.note: Illyrius is born to Cadmus and Harmonia during their Illyrian rule.

Ilus.note: Ilus belongs to Hector's direct Trojan royal ancestry.
Paris descends from Ilus through Laomedon and Priam.
Ilus is Priam's grandfather in the principal Trojan genealogy.

Imbrius.note: Ajax kills Imbrius during reciprocal fighting over bodies.

Inachus.note: Inachus is Io’s father in a major Argive genealogy.

Ino.note: Ino, later the sea-goddess Leucothea, is Cadmus’s daughter.
The maddened Ino attacks Pentheus and helps tear him apart.
Ino is Semele’s sister in the Cadmean genealogy.
Ino falsely claims Semele conceived by a mortal and lied about Zeus.
After Semele dies, Ino nurses her infant Dionysus at Brasiae.

Ino-Leucothea.note: She gives Odysseus a veil enabling him to survive shipwreck.

Ino/Leucothea.note: Sisyphus receives or finds the dead child of his sister-in-law Ino.

Iolaus.myth: Iolaus and Alcmene share the Cynosarges cult group
Iolaus.note: Iolaus receives cult alongside Alcmene, Heracles, and Hebe without a surviving direct exchange.
Iolaus cauterizes the Hydra’s severed necks while assisting Heracles.

Iole.myth: Alcmene recounts Heracles’ birth to Iole
Iole.note: The aged Alcmene tells Iole about her obstructed labor and Galanthis’ intervention.
Deianira pities the captive but fears that Heracles will replace her.

Iphianassa.note: Homer names Iphianassa as Agamemnon's daughter.
Agamemnon offers one of his daughters, including Iphianassa, to Achilles.
The Iliad names Iphianassa among Agamemnon’s daughters by implication.

Iphicles.note: Alcmene and Amphitryon are the biological parents of Iphicles.

Iphicles.myth: Amphitryon tests the twins with serpents
Iphicles.note: Amphitryon endangers Iphicles and Heracles with snakes to determine which infant is his.
Iphicles and Atalanta appear together in hunter or Argonaut catalogues.
Iphicles appears with Meleager among the assembled hunters.

Iphiclus.note: Iphiclus is Leda’s brother in the Aetolian genealogy.
Protesilaus is identified as the son of Iphiclus.

Iphiclus son of Thestius.note: Meleager's maternal relative Iphiclus accompanies him among the Argonauts.

Iphimachus.note: The shepherd Iphimachus tends the abandoned and wounded Philoctetes.

Iphimede.note: The Hesiodic Catalogue names Iphimede as Clytemnestra and Agamemnon’s daughter.

Iphis.note: Achilles allotted the captive Iphis to Patroclus, and she shares his bed.

Irus/Arnaeus.note: Disguised Odysseus defeats Irus in a staged boxing contest.

Isander.note: Isander is one of Bellerophon’s three children in Homer.

Isis.myth: Io becomes the Egyptian goddess Isis
Isis.note: Greek and Roman writers identify restored Io with the Egyptian goddess.

Ismene.note: Ismene is Antigone's sister in all relevant genealogies.
Antigone requests Ismene's help, then rejects her attempted shared guilt.
The sisters accompany Oedipus, suffer capture, and mourn together.
Ismene is Oedipus’s daughter in fifth-century tragedy.
Ismene brings Oedipus political news and oracular information from Thebes.
Theseus recovers Ismene from Creon’s men and restores her to Oedipus.

Itone.note: Itone appears as an alternative wife of Minos.

Itymoneus.note: Young Nestor kills Itymoneus while raiding Epeian cattle.

Itys.note: Procne is the mother of Itys by Tereus.
Philomela is the maternal aunt of Itys.
Procne kills Itys; Philomela participates in cutting up and cooking him.

Jocasta.note: Jocasta is Antigone's mother in the dominant tragic genealogy.
Antigone witnesses or laments Jocasta's death during the Theban catastrophe.
Jocasta, called Epicaste by Homer, is Oedipus’s biological mother.
Oedipus unknowingly marries his mother after killing Laius.

Kalos.note: Pausanias preserves Kalos as the local Athenian name of Daedalus's murdered nephew.

Ketos.note: Andromeda actively helps Perseus fight the sea monster by supplying stones.
Andromeda is exposed as prey for the sea monster sent against Ethiopia.

Kronos.note: Consultants sacrifice to Kronos before entering Trophonius’ oracle.

Labdacus.note: Cadmus is Labdacus’s dynastic ancestor through Polydorus.
Oedipus descends from Labdacus through his father Laius.

Laelaps.myth: Amphitryon deploys Laelaps against the Teumessian fox
Laelaps.note: Amphitryon uses the infallible hound to pursue the creature fated never to be caught.

Laertes.note: Laertes and Atalanta fight, suffer wounds, and receive Medea’s healing together.
Odysseus initially conceals his identity while testing his father.
After recognition, Odysseus and Laertes fight together.
Penelope ostensibly weaves Laertes’s burial cloth to postpone remarriage.
Laertes marries Anticleia while she is allegedly pregnant by Sisyphus.
Telemachus fights beside Laertes and Odysseus against the suitors’ relatives.

Laius.note: Cadmus is Laius’s dynastic ancestor through Polydorus and Labdacus.
Laius is Oedipus’s biological father and predecessor in the Labdacid line.
Oedipus kills Laius without knowing that Laius is his father.
Pelops curses Laius for abducting and sexually violating Chrysippus.
Tiresias conducts necromancy to summon Laius’s ghost.

Lampus.note: Later genealogical systematization lists Lampus among Priam's siblings.

Laocoon of Calydon.note: The older Laocoon accompanies and guards the youthful Meleager.

Laodice.note: Homer names Laodice among Agamemnon's daughters.
Laodice is included among Cassandra’s Trojan sisters.
Laodice is named among Agamemnon’s daughters, with no direct maternal episode.
Xanthus reportedly said Laodice was renamed Electra because she remained unmarried.
Apollodorus lists Laodice among Hecuba's children.
Laodice is Polyxena’s sister in mythographical catalogues.
Laodice is listed among Priam's daughters by Hecuba.

Laodocus.note: Laodocus is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Laomedon.note: Laomedon is Priam's predecessor and Hector's grandfather in the standard genealogy.
Memnon descends from Laomedon through his father Tithonus.
Laomedon is Paris's great-grandfather through Priam.
Penthesilea's bones are buried beside Laomedon's without a living encounter.
Priam is Laomedon's son and successor after Heracles sacks Troy.
Aeacus helps construct the Trojan wall associated with Laomedon’s rule.

Laonome.note: Some late genealogies make Laonome the daughter of Amphitryon and Alcmene.
One mythographic genealogy names Laonome as Amphitryon’s mother.

Laothoe.note: Laothoe is Priam's wife and mother of Lycaon and Polydorus.

Lapithes.note: Diodorus’s Thessalian genealogy makes Ixion a descendant of Lapithes.

Las.note: A Laconian variant says Patroclus, rather than Achilles, killed Las.

Latinus.note: Later genealogy names Latinus as Odysseus' son by Circe.

Leiodes.note: Leiodes and Telemachus both attempt the bow, without a personal confrontation.

Leonteus.note: Hyginus gives Leonteus as Ixion’s father.

Leontophonus.note: Leontophonus is his son by the daughter of Thoas.

Leopold Bloom.note: Joyce maps Leopold Bloom broadly onto Odysseus in a modern urban reinvention.

Lernus.note: Penthesilea kills Lernus during her battlefield rampage.

Lethe.note: Consultants drink from Lethe before descending to Trophonius.

Leucane.note: Leucane is occasionally named as Io’s mother in late genealogies.

Libya.note: Libya is Io’s granddaughter through Epaphus.

Lichas.note: Lichas initially conceals why Heracles destroyed Oechalia and brought Iole home.
Deianira entrusts Heracles’ anointed ceremonial garment to Lichas for delivery.

Licymnius.myth: Licymnius accompanies Alcmene and Amphitryon into exile
Licymnius.note: Licymnius travels with the couple after Sthenelus expels them.

Linus.note: Linus and Orpheus are paired among the primordial singers.
Some unstable learned traditions make Linus a teacher of Orpheus.

Liriope.note: The Naiad Liriope is Narcissus' mother.

Locrus.note: A fragment links Locrus's Lelegians with stones Zeus gave Deucalion.

Lycaon.note: Achilles kills the recaptured Lycaon despite his supplication and ransom appeal.
Lycaon is Callisto’s father in the dominant Arcadian genealogy.
Lycaon's crime indirectly causes the flood survived by Deucalion and Pyrrha.
Lycaon is Priam's son by Laothoe.

Lycastus.note: In Diodorus’s two-Minos scheme, Lycastus is Minos’s son or descendant.

Lycomedes.note: Lycomedes shelters Achilles while Thetis conceals him among the king’s daughters.
Lycomedes pushes Theseus from a cliff, fearing him or supporting Menestheus.

Lycurgus.note: The chorus parallels Antigone with imprisoned Lycurgus, punished for opposing Dionysus.

Lycurgus of Nemea.note: Amphiaraus participates in the dispute after the death of Lycurgus’ son.

Lycus.myth: Lycus threatens Amphitryon and Heracles’ family
Lycus.note: Amphitryon resists the usurper who intends to kill him, Megara, and the children.
Lycus hosts the company and promises a local cult for the Dioscuri.
Lycus is one of Diomedes’ companions transformed into a bird.

Lycus son of Pandion.note: The fellow exile Lycus joins Sarpedon, after which outsiders call the people Lycians.

Lynceus.note: Lynceus uses extraordinary sight to aid the company’s navigation and searching.
Lynceus and Atalanta appear together in hunter or Argonaut catalogues.
Lynceus joins Io’s descendant line through his marriage to Hypermestra.
Lynceus appears with Meleager among the hunters in later catalogues.
Lynceus and Meleager sail together as Argonauts.

Lysianassa.note: Lysianassa, daughter of Polybus, is Adrastus's mother in the Sicyonian genealogy.

Lysidice.note: A variant genealogy names Lysidice as Alcmene’s mother.
Lysidice is a daughter of Pelops in later genealogical traditions.

Lysimache.note: Lysimache, daughter of Abas, is Adrastus's mother in one genealogy.
Lysimache is listed among Priam's daughters by other women.

Lysithous.note: Lysithous is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Lyssa.note: Personified Madness infects or incites the hounds that destroy Actaeon.

Lyssa.myth: Lyssa drives Heracles mad and endangers Amphitryon
Lyssa.note: Lyssa’s attack on Heracles indirectly causes his family’s massacre and nearly costs Amphitryon his life.
Lyssa deranges Heracles at Iris’ command, causing his catastrophic violence.

Macaria.note: Later genealogies infer Deianira’s maternity, though Euripides names only Heracles as parent.

Machaereus.note: Apollo’s priest Machaereus kills Neoptolemus during a dispute over sacrificial meat.
Machaereus first buries Neoptolemus beneath the Delphic temple threshold.

Machaon.note: Machaon treats the arrow wound Menelaus receives after the truce breaks.
Nestor carries the wounded healer from battle and hosts him in his hut.
Penthesilea kills the Greek physician-hero in one unstable victim tradition.
Machaon cures Philoctetes after his return to the Greek army.

Maenalus.note: Maenalus is Atalanta’s father in Euripides’ genealogy.

Maeon.note: Later reconstruction associates Antigone and Haemon's unnamed son with Maeon.

Manto.note: Niobe interrupts the rite Manto orders for Leto, Apollo, and Diana.
Manto is securely named as Tiresias’s prophetic daughter.
Manto guides Tiresias and describes sacrificial signs he cannot see.

Maraphius.note: A later genealogical variant names Maraphius among Helen’s children.
A genealogical tradition names Maraphius as Menelaus’ son.

Marathonios.note: Hecataeus's competing genealogy names Marathonios as Deucalion's son.

Mares of Diomedes.note: Heracles captures the man-eating mares after defeating their owner.

Marsyas.note: Midas prefers Marsyas' music to Apollo's in Hyginus' variant.

Marygold.note: Hawthorne invents Marygold as Midas' beloved daughter.
Midas accidentally turns his daughter into a golden statue.

Mecisteus.note: Mecisteus is Adrastus's brother or kinsman in later genealogy.
Mecisteus appears with Amphiaraus in variant catalogues of the Seven.

Medeius.note: Cinaethon’s genealogy names Medeius as a child of Jason and Medea.
Medeius is Medea's son by Jason in the earliest genealogy.
Cinaethon names Medeius and Eriopis as Medea's children by Jason.

Medesicaste.note: Medesicaste is listed among Priam's daughters by other women.

Medon.note: Hellanicus, as cited by Pausanias, names Medon as Electra’s son by Pylades.
Medon commands Philoctetes’ Thessalian contingent while he remains wounded on Lemnos.
Telemachus testifies that Medon acted unwillingly and saves his life.

Medus.note: Later tradition makes Medus Medea's son by Aegeus.
Medea travels east with Medus, whose conquests explain the Medes' name.

Megapenthes.note: Megapenthes expels Helen after Menelaus’s death in the Rhodian tradition.
Megapenthes is Menelaus’ son by an unnamed enslaved woman.
Perseus exchanges Argos for Megapenthes’ kingdom of Tiryns.
An isolated variant says Megapenthes kills Perseus to avenge Proetus.

Megara.myth: Amphitryon protects Megara during Lycus’ usurpation
Megara.note: Amphitryon remains with his daughter-in-law Megara as Lycus prepares to execute them.
The Cyzicene epigram identifies Megara as Ixion’s murdered mother.

Megareus.note: Megareus comes to aid Nisus and dies fighting Minos’s forces.

Megisto.note: Araethus’ regional genealogy replaces Callisto with Megisto, Ceteus’ daughter and Lycaon’s granddaughter.

Melampus.note: Melampus accompanies Admetus when they greet their kinsman Jason.
Amphiaraus descends from the seer Melampus through Antiphates and Oicles.

Melanion.note: Melanion wins Atalanta’s race using apples supplied by Aphrodite.
Melanion marries Atalanta and fathers Parthenopaeus in the Arcadian tradition.
Atalanta and Melanion have sanctuary intercourse and are transformed together.
Milanion persistently pursues Atalanta and suffers Hylaeus’s wound.

Melanippe.note: Learned genealogical consolidation sometimes includes Melanippe among her sisters.
Melanippe is Apollodorus’s alternative identity for Theseus’s captured Amazon.
In Apollodorus’s alternative version, Theseus captures Melanippe.

Melanippus.note: Melanippus is installed as Adrastus's cultic enemy and receives his former sacrifices.
Amphiaraus kills or decapitates Melanippus and gives his head to Tydeus.
Patroclus kills Melanippus during his final assault toward Troy.
Melanippus is listed among Priam's sons by other women.
Melanippus is Theseus’s son by Perigune.

Melanthius.note: Odysseus' allies mutilate and kill the goatherd who aided the suitors.
Melanthius arms the suitors and is captured by Telemachus’ loyal faction.
Telemachus participates in or supervises Melanthius’ mutilation and death.

Melantho.note: Later regional genealogies call Melantho a daughter of Deucalion.
Melantho is included among the household women Telemachus condemns and hangs.

Melanthus.note: Scholastic tradition gives Melanthus as one of Laocoön’s sons.

Melicertes/Palaemon.note: Melicertes is Sisyphus's nephew through Athamas.
Sisyphus buries Melicertes and establishes funeral honors and games for him.

Memnonides.myth: Birds arise from Memnon’s funeral pyre
Memnonides.note: Birds arise from the smoke and ashes of Memnon’s pyre.
The birds annually clean, wet, fight over, or die at Memnon’s tomb.

Menesthes.note: Hector kills Menesthes during the Trojan War.

Menestheus.note: Ajax answers Menestheus’s request for help against the Lycians.
Menestheus exploits Theseus’s absence and displaces him from Athens.

Menesthius.note: Paris kills or helps kill Menesthius, depending on textual identification.
Menesthius commands one Myrmidon company under Patroclus.

Menippe.note: A Byzantine compilation names Menippe, daughter of Thamyris, as Orpheus’s mother.

Menippus.note: Menippus is shown Narcissus among the famous beauties in Hades.
Menippus mocks Tantalus for fearing thirst despite being a bodiless shade.

Menoeceus.note: Oedipus is Menoeceus’s maternal grandson through Jocasta.
One scholastic genealogy makes Pentheus Menoeceus’ grandfather through Oclasus.
Tiresias names Menoeceus as the required sacrificial victim.

Meriones.note: Meriones opposes Hector's forces, though their direct contact is limited.
Meriones helps Menelaus carry Patroclus’ corpse from the battlefield.
Meriones helps carry Patroclus’ corpse away and organizes funeral wood.

Mermerus.note: Mermerus is commonly named as a son of Jason and Medea.
Mermerus is a son of Medea and Jason.
In the canonical tragedy, Medea deliberately kills her son.
In Corinthian variants, Mermerus is killed by Corinthians rather than Medea.
The Naupactia says a lioness kills Mermerus while he is hunting.

Merope.note: Merope is Oedipus’s foster mother, whom he believes biological.
Hyginus' alternative genealogy makes the Oceanid Merope Phaethon's mother.
The Pleiad Merope is Sisyphus's wife.
Sisyphus orders his wife to omit funeral rites, enabling his deceptive return.

Mestor.note: Mestor is a son of Andromeda and Perseus.
Mestor is listed among the sons of Perseus and Andromeda.
Mestor is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Metharme.note: Pygmalion, king of Cyprus, is Metharme’s father.

Methone.note: Methone is an alternative mother in later genealogical tradition.

Metion.note: Diodorus names Metion as Daedalus's father.

Metope.note: Apollodorus records Metope as Hecuba's mother.
Aeacus is Metope’s grandson through Aegina.

Miletus.note: Minos and Sarpedon contest the favor of Miletus in one version.
Miletus prefers Sarpedon to Minos, contributing to Sarpedon's exile.

Moirai.note: The Moirai join Eileithyia in preventing Alcmene from giving birth.

Moirai/Fates.note: The Fates permit Admetus to escape death if another dies voluntarily.
Apollo intoxicates the Fates and obtains alteration of Admetus’ death-lot.

Molion.note: Penthesilea kills Molion during her battlefield rampage.

Molos.note: Molos is Minos’s son or illegitimate descendant and father of Meriones.

Molossus.note: Andromache surrenders from sanctuary when Menelaus threatens her hidden son.
Molossus is Neoptolemus’ son by Andromache and a Molossian ancestor.
Molossus is Peleus’ great-grandson through Achilles and Neoptolemus.
Peleus rescues his great-grandson Molossus from Menelaus’ attempted killing.

Molpadia.note: Theseus kills Molpadia after she kills Antiope in one account.

Mopsus.note: Mopsus serves as the company’s seer before dying from a snake bite.
Mopsus serves as a seer under Jason and dies from a Libyan snakebite.
One inconsistent genealogy makes Mopsus Tiresias’s descendant through Manto.

Mulius.note: Patroclus kills Mulius during his final assault toward Troy.

Musaeus.note: Musaeus is variously Orpheus’s disciple, recipient, companion, or successor.
Some learned genealogies make Musaeus the son of Orpheus.

Mygdon.note: Priam recalls Mygdon and the Phrygian host during the Amazon war.

Mylius.note: Mylius is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Myrmidons.note: Zeus transforms ants into the Myrmidons who become Aeacus’s subjects.
Aeacus receives a restored population of Myrmidons after dreaming ants became people.

Myrtilus.note: Myrtilus conspires with Pelops or Hippodamia to sabotage Oenomaus’s chariot.
Pelops refuses Myrtilus the promised kingdom, payment, or sexual reward.
Pelops throws Myrtilus into the sea near Cape Geraestus.
Dying Myrtilus curses Pelops and his descendants with dynastic ruin.

Myrto.note: Late genealogical compilations sometimes identify Myrto as Patroclus’ sister.

Nauplius.note: Nauplius is Palamedes’s stable father, though genealogies disagree about which Nauplius.
Nauplius subverts Greek households and lights the fatal Caphereus beacon in revenge.

Nausicaa.note: Nausicaa finds, clothes, and directs Odysseus to the Phaeacian palace.
Dictys makes Nausicaa the wife of Telemachus.

Nausimedon.note: Nausimedon is Palamedes’s brother in mythographic genealogy.

Nausinous.note: A later genealogy makes Nausinous his son by Calypso.

Nausithous.note: A later genealogy makes Nausithous his son by Calypso.

Nebrophonus.note: Some later sources name Nebrophonus as Jason and Hypsipyle’s son.

Neleus.note: Neleus is Nestor’s father and predecessor as ruler of Pylos.
Sisyphus conceals the location of Neleus's grave, even from Nestor.

Nephalion.note: Nephalion is attributed to Minos by later genealogical traditions.

Nephele.note: Ixion mistakes the manufactured cloud-image for Hera and has intercourse with it.

Nessus.note: Nessus ferries Deianira and then sexually assaults or abducts her.
The dying centaur tricks Deianira into preserving lethal material as a fidelity charm.
Heracles shoots Nessus with a Hydra-poisoned arrow after the centaur attacks Deianira.
Nessus engineers Heracles’ death by deceiving Deianira about his poisoned blood.
Hyginus calls Nessus a son of Ixion and the Cloud.

Nicippe.note: Nicippe is a daughter of Pelops in later genealogical traditions.

Nicostratus.note: Later genealogical traditions name Nicostratus as Helen’s son.
Nicostratus joins Megapenthes in expelling Helen after Menelaus’s death.
Variant traditions make Nicostratus a son of Menelaus.

Niobids.note: Niobe is mother of the variably numbered Niobids.

Nireus.note: Nireus and Narcissus are jointly listed among the beautiful dead.

Nomia.myth: Callisto rests beside Nomia in Hades
Nomia.note: Polygnotus depicted Callisto beside Nomia, with Callisto’s feet resting on her knees.

Nycteus.note: Asius’ alternative genealogy makes Callisto the daughter of Nycteus.
Nycteus is one of Diomedes’ companions transformed into a bird.

Oceanids.myth: Oceanids hear and lament Io’s suffering
Oceanids.note: The Oceanid chorus listens sympathetically as Io recounts her persecution.

Oclasus.note: One scholastic genealogy makes Oclasus the son of Pentheus.

Ocnus.note: One inconsistent genealogy makes Ocnus Tiresias’s descendant through Manto.

Odites.note: Odites is Deianira’s son by Heracles.

Oeagrus.note: Oeagrus is Orpheus’s father in the dominant Argonautic genealogy.

Oeax.note: Oeax falsely or maliciously reports that Cassandra is arriving as Clytemnestra’s rival.
Oeax falsely convinces Aegialeia that Diomedes returns with a preferred Trojan woman.
Oeax is Palamedes’s brother in tragic and mythographic tradition.
Oeax inscribes Palamedes’s death on oar blades and casts them toward Nauplius.

Oeneus.note: Atalanta joins the heroic response to Oeneus’s summons against the boar.
Oeneus of Calydon is Diomedes’ paternal grandfather.
Diomedes and Alcmaeon kill most usurpers and restore the elderly Oeneus.
Oeneus is Meleager's father in the ordinary genealogy.
Oeneus begs his withdrawn son to return and defend Calydon.
Peleus answers the Calydonian ruler’s summons to hunt the destructive boar.

Oenomaus.note: Hector kills the Achaean warrior Oenomaus during the Trojan War.
Pelops challenges Oenomaus in the deadly race for Hippodamia.
Pelops defeats Oenomaus through divine aid or Myrtilus’s sabotage.
In one variant, Pelops directly kills Oenomaus during the contest.

Oenone.note: The Idaean nymph Oenone is Paris's first wife or lover.
Paris abandons Oenone despite his earlier declarations and her warning.
Oenone initially refuses to heal Paris, then repents after his death.

Ogygus.note: Ogygus rules the Ectenes before Cadmus’s arrival in Pausanias’s local history.

Oicles.note: Oicles is Amphiaraus’ father in the dominant genealogy.

Opheltes.note: Amphiaraus interprets the infant’s death as doom’s beginning and renames him Archemorus.

Opheltes.myth: Funeral of Opheltes and founding of Nemean Games
Opheltes.note: After a serpent kills Opheltes, the Seven conduct his funeral games.

Opheltes/Archemorus.myth: Death and funeral games at Nemea
Opheltes/Archemorus.note: Adrastus helps bury Opheltes and institutes funeral games after the child's death.

Opheltius.note: Hector kills Opheltius during the Trojan War.

Opites.note: Hector kills Opites during the Trojan War.

Oreithyia.note: Oreithyia gives Penthesilea a supernatural horse during her Thracian visit.

Oresbius.note: Hector kills Oresbius during the Trojan War.

Ornytion.note: Ornytion is named as a son of Sisyphus.

Orus.note: Hector kills Orus during the Trojan War.

Other Centaurs.note: Centaurs threaten the disarmed Peleus after Acastus abandons him on Pelion.

Other sons of Thestius.note: Meleager kills his maternal uncles amid confused battle; their names are unstated.

Othryoneus.note: Othryoneus seeks Cassandra in marriage but dies before fulfilling his bargain.

Otrera.note: Imperial mythographers identify Otrera as Penthesilea's mother.

Otreus.note: Priam recalls being present with Otreus's Phrygian forces during an Amazon attack.

Palamaon.note: Pausanias preserves Palamaon as Daedalus's father.

Pammon.note: Apollodorus lists Pammon among Hecuba's sons.
Pammon is listed among Priam's sons by Hecuba.

Pandareus.note: In parallel traditions, the analogous sisters Aëdon and Chelidon are daughters of Pandareus.
Pandareus entrusts the stolen golden dog to Tantalus, implicating them both.

Pandarus.note: Pandarus wounds Diomedes with an arrow before their fatal encounter.
Diomedes kills Pandarus with a spear through the face.
Pandarus shoots and wounds Menelaus, violating the sworn treaty.
Pandarus breaks the truce after Paris's duel, though no direct exchange survives.

Pandion.note: Pandion is the father of Philomela and Procne.
Pandion entrusts Philomela to Tereus after Tereus promises to protect her.

Pandora II.note: Pandora II is named as Deucalion's daughter.

Panopeus.note: Panopeus serves as one of Amphitryon’s allies against the Taphians and Teleboans.

Pans.note: A classical vase places a chorus of Pans beneath Pandora’s creation scene.

Paphos.note: Paphos is born to Pygmalion and the animated ivory woman.

Parthenopaeus.note: Parthenopaeus is Adrastus's brother in Pseudo-Apollodorus's genealogy.
Parthenopaeus is one of Adrastus's champions against Thebes.

Parthenopaeus.myth: Funeral oration for the fallen champions
Parthenopaeus.note: Adrastus praises Parthenopaeus after the recovery of the Argive dead.
Parthenopaeus and Amphiaraus appear together among the Seven and in artistic councils.
Parthenopaeus, one of the Seven against Thebes, is Atalanta’s son.
Hyginus makes Parthenopaeus Meleager's son, usually through Atalanta.

Pedasus.note: Sarpedon's missed cast strikes and kills Pedasus, the mortal horse in Patroclus' team.

Peiren.note: Peiren replaces Deliades as Bellerophon’s homicide victim in one version.
Peiren or Piras is Io’s father in an archaic genealogy.

Peirithous.note: The ordinary later genealogy makes Peirithous the son of Ixion and Dia.
Nestor recalls Peirithous as his comrade against the Centaurs.
Theseus and Peirithous initially fight before admiring one another.
Theseus fights beside Peirithous and the Lapiths against the Centaurs.
Theseus and Peirithous jointly abduct the young Helen for forced marriage.
Theseus accompanies Peirithous into Hades to seize Persephone.

Peisander.note: Menelaus kills Peisander after savage close combat.
Peisander commands one Myrmidon company under Patroclus.

Peision.note: Pindaric scholia and lexicographic tradition preserve this unstable father-name.

Peisistratus.note: Menelaus entertains Peisistratus when he accompanies Telemachus to Sparta.
Peisistratus is Nestor’s son and Telemachus’ appointed escort.
Peisistratus escorts Telemachus from Pylos to Sparta and back.

Peitho.note: Peitho and the Charites place golden necklaces upon Pandora.

Pelagon.note: Pelagon removes Tlepolemus' spear from Sarpedon's thigh after companions carry him away.

Pelias.note: Alcestis is securely attested as a daughter of Pelias.
Pelias requires Alcestis’ suitor to yoke a lion and boar.
Amphiaraus competes in the funeral games held for Pelias.

Pelias.myth: The quest for the Golden Fleece
Pelias.note: Pelias usurps Aeson’s rule and sends Jason on the lethal fleece quest.
Jason seeks vengeance, while Medea tricks Pelias’s daughters into killing him.
Medea engineers Pelias's death by deceiving his daughters.
Peleus competes in games held after Pelias’ death.

Pelops, son of Agamemnon.note: Pelops is Cassandra’s infant twin son by Agamemnon.

Pelorus.note: Pelorus survives the Spartoi conflict and becomes a Theban ancestor.

Pemphredo.note: Perseus intercepts Pemphredo’s shared eye to compel directions to the nymphs.

Peneus.note: Heracles diverts the river Peneus through Augeas’ cattle-yard.

Penthilus.note: Penthilus is Orestes’ illegitimate son by Erigone.

Perdix.note: Jealous Daedalus throws his gifted pupil and nephew from Minerva's citadel.

Pergamus.note: Pausanias names Pergamus as Andromache’s son by Neoptolemus.
Andromache accompanies her son when he conquers Teuthrania and founds Pergamum.
Pausanias names Pergamus as Neoptolemus’ son by Andromache.

Periboea.note: Periboea replaces Merope as Oedipus’s foster mother in this variant.
The naiad Periboea is Penelope’s mother in Apollodorus’s genealogy.

Periclymene.note: Later genealogical traditions variously name Periclymene as Admetus’ mother.

Periclymenus.note: Periclymenus fights Adrastus's army and pursues Amphiaraus during the rout.
Periclymenus pursues Amphiaraus and nearly strikes him before Zeus intervenes.
The Poseidon-gifted shapeshifter appears among the company in the Pindaric tradition.
Heracles kills the shape-shifting Periclymenus with Athena’s assistance.
Periclymenus and Nestor are sons of Neleus and Chloris.

Perigune.note: Theseus finds Sinis’s daughter Perigune and fathers Melanippus with her.
Perigune is a partner of Theseus and mother of Melanippus.

Perilaus.note: Perilaus acts as Orestes’ accuser in a localized Arcadian proceeding.

Perimela.note: Diodorus names Perimela, daughter of Amythaon, as Ixion’s mother.

Perimele.note: Late genealogical lists name Perimele among the couple’s children.

Perimus.note: Patroclus kills Perimus during his final assault toward Troy.

Periopis.note: An alternative Apollodoran genealogy names Periopis as Patroclus’ mother.

Periphetes.note: Hector kills Periphetes during the Trojan War.
Theseus kills the club-bearing robber with his own weapon.
Theseus takes and thereafter carries Periphetes’s club.

Pero.myth: Callisto and Pero appear in Hades
Pero.note: Polygnotus depicted Pero together with Callisto and Nomia in the Delphic underworld.
Pero and Nestor are children of Neleus and Chloris.

Perseis.note: Medea is Perseis's great-granddaughter through Helios and Aeëtes.

Persepolis.note: Telemachus fathers Persepolis or Perseptolis with Polycaste.

Persinous.note: Penthesilea kills Persinous during her battlefield rampage.

Phaea.note: Theseus kills Phaea, portrayed as a monstrous sow or female robber.

Phaeacians.note: The Phaeacians host the company and witness Jason and Medea’s marriage.
The Phaeacians convey Rhadamanthus to Euboea and back in one day.

Phalanx.note: Phalanx is Arachne's brother in the Attic variant.
Arachne and her brother Phalanx have incestuous intercourse and are jointly punished.

Phamenoph.myth: Competing names for the vocal statue
Phamenoph.note: Pausanias says Egyptians called the statue Phamenoph while Greeks called it Memnon.

Pharmacides.note: Hera’s regional agents prevent Alcmene’s delivery until Historis tricks them.

Phemius.note: Telemachus intercedes and saves the unwilling bard from execution.

Phereclus.note: Phereclus builds the ships Paris uses despite knowing their disastrous destiny.

Pheres.note: Admetus is the son of Pheres in the standard genealogy.
Pheres refuses to die for Admetus; father and son exchange accusations.
Pheres is commonly named as a son of Jason and Medea.
Pheres is a son of Medea and Jason.
In the canonical tragedy, Medea deliberately kills her son.
In a local variant, Corinthians kill Pheres for carrying Medea's gifts.

Philaemon.note: Philaemon is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Philaeus.note: One Athenian genealogy makes Philaeus Ajax’s son.
Another genealogy makes Philaeus Eurysaces’ son and Ajax’s descendant.

Philoetius.note: The loyal cattleman Philoetius fights beside Odysseus.
The loyal cattle-herd joins Telemachus’ faction in battle and punishment.

Philonoe.note: Philonoe is the daughter of Leda and Tyndareus.

Philottus.note: Philottus is Niobe's husband in the Parthenius variant.

Philyra.note: The cyclic Nostoi names Philyra as Palamedes’s mother.

Phineus.note: Phineus is named as Andromeda’s earlier betrothed.
Phineus contests her marriage through conspiracy or an armed wedding assault.
Phineus' family tragedy is invoked as an analogue for Antigone's suffering.
The company drives away his tormentors; Phineus then instructs it on the route.
Phineus teaches the company how to test and pass the clashing rocks.
Phineus advises Jason to test the Clashing Rocks with a dove.
Perseus battles Phineus after the rival claimant attacks the wedding feast.
Perseus petrifies Phineus with Medusa’s severed head.

Phlegon.myth: Phaethon loses control of the solar horses
Phlegon.note: Phlegon bolts with the team when Phaethon cannot govern the chariot.

Phlegyas.note: Servian and scholiastic genealogies make Phlegyas Ixion’s father.

Phocus.note: Phocus, son of Aeacus and Psamathe, is Peleus’ half-brother.
Some versions make Peleus kill Phocus deliberately or accidentally; others blame Telamon.
Aeacus fathers Phocus with the Nereid Psamathe.

Phoenix.note: Peleus entrusts Achilles to Phoenix for instruction in speech and action.
Phoenix counsels Achilles and urges him to accept Agamemnon’s restitution.
Phoenix and Ajax serve together in the embassy to Achilles.
Phoenix is Cadmus’s father in a competing epic and genealogical tradition.
Phoenix is Cadmus’s brother in the canonical Agenorid genealogy.
Phoenix accompanies or guides Neoptolemus in some cyclic summaries.
Neoptolemus buries Phoenix after his death during the overland return.
Phoenix commands one Myrmidon company under Patroclus.
Peleus receives and honors the exiled Phoenix in Phthia.
Peleus assigns Phoenix to rear and instruct Achilles.
Phoenix is named among the participants or witnesses at Polyxena’s sacrifice.

Pholegander.note: Pholegander is a child of Minos in regional genealogy.

Pholus.myth: Centaur fight during the boar labour
Pholus.note: Pholus hosts Heracles before accidentally killing himself with Heracles’ poisoned arrow.

Phorbas.note: Ixion kills Phorbas for murdering his mother after she rejected him.

Phorcys.note: Ajax kills Phorcys while defending Patroclus’s corpse.

Phrixus’ sons.note: The company rescues the shipwrecked brothers, who then guide it toward Colchis.
The rescued sons of Phrixus guide and advise the company on entering Colchis.

Phylacus.note: Later genealogies make Phylacus Protesilaus's paternal grandfather and dynastic ancestor.

Phylonoe.note: Phylonoe is Clytemnestra’s sister in one reconstruction of the fragmentary genealogy.

Pielus.note: Pausanias names Pielus as Andromache’s son by Neoptolemus.
Pausanias names Pielus as Neoptolemus’ son and Epirot successor.

Pirithous.note: Pirithous and Atalanta participate together in later hunter catalogues.
Pirithous shares Theseus’s abduction scheme and loses the lot for Helen.
Heracles tries but fails, or is forbidden, to free Pirithous.
Pirithous appears with Meleager among the assembled hunters.
Pirithous and Meleager participate in a fragmentarily preserved underworld dialogue.

Pisidice.note: Later mythography names Pisidice as a daughter of Nestor.

Pittheus.note: Hippolytus is raised in Pittheus’ Troezenian household and comes from his palace.
Pittheus is Pelops’s son in the dominant Troezenian genealogy.
Pittheus is Theseus’s maternal grandfather and fosterer at Troezen.

Plastene.note: The local Sipylus tradition identifies Plastene as Pelops’s mother.

Pleisthenes.note: Some later genealogies make Pleisthenes his biological father.
Later genealogical traditions name Pleisthenes as Helen’s son.
An alternative genealogy makes Pleisthenes Menelaus’ biological father.

Plexippus.note: Plexippus seizes or contests the trophy awarded to Atalanta.
Plexippus is Leda’s brother in the Aetolian genealogy.
Meleager kills his maternal uncle Plexippus during the trophy dispute.

Pluto/Plouto.note: The female figure Pluto or Plouto is Tantalus’s mother.

Podalirius.note: Podalirius heals Philoctetes in later accounts, replacing Machaon.

Podarces.note: Penthesilea mortally wounds Podarces after he kills her companion Clonie.
Podarces is Protesilaus's younger brother and succeeds him as commander.
A divergent Phylacid genealogy apparently makes Protesilaus and Podarces cousins.

Podes.note: Menelaus kills Podes, a companion of Hector.

Poeas.note: In an alternate tradition Poeas lights Heracles’ pyre after Deianira’s death.
Poeas is consistently named as Philoctetes’ father.
Poeas gives Philoctetes the bow previously received from Heracles.

Polemusa.note: Polemusa accompanies Penthesilea and is killed by Achilles.

Polites.note: Apollodorus lists Polites among Hecuba's sons.
Pyrrhus pursues and kills Polites before his father’s eyes.
Priam witnesses Neoptolemus kill Polites immediately before his own murder.

Polybus.note: Polybus is Adrastus's maternal grandfather in the Sicyonian genealogy.
Polybus hosts Adrastus or precedes him as king; Adrastus inherits his throne.
Polybus raises Oedipus as his son; Oedipus believes him biological.

Polycaste.note: Polycaste is Nestor’s unmarried daughter in his Pylian household.
Polycaste is Penelope’s mother in a competing genealogical tradition.
Polycaste bathes and anoints Telemachus during his stay with Nestor.
A variant makes Polycaste Telemachus’ partner and mother of his son.

Polydamas.note: Hector rejects Polydamas' sound advice to withdraw, preparing the Trojan collapse.

Polydectes.note: Polydectes’ contrived gift demand sends Perseus after Medusa’s head.
Perseus returns with Medusa’s head and kills or petrifies Polydectes.

Polydeuces.note: Polydeuces and Admetus are co-members of later heroic expedition lists.
Polydeuces sails with the company and defeats its hostile Bebrycian challenger.
Polydeuces is Helen’s brother, commonly assigned divine paternity.
Polydeuces invades Attica with Castor and recovers Helen from Theseus.
Polydeuces intervenes with Castor to secure Helen’s escape and future divinity.
Polydeuces accompanies Jason and defeats Amycus during the expedition.
Polydeuces is Helen’s brother and therefore Menelaus’ brother-in-law.
Polydeuces is Orpheus’s fellow Argonaut and participates in Orpheus-led rites or songs.
Polydeuces joins Castor in recovering Helen and capturing Aethra.

Polydora.note: Later genealogy makes Polydora the daughter of Meleager and Cleopatra.
Polydora is Peleus’ daughter in the principal genealogy.
The Cypria names Polydora, rather than Laodamia, as Protesilaus's wife.

Polydorus.note: Polydorus is Cadmus’s son and dynastic heir.
Polydorus is included among Cassandra’s Trojan brothers.
Polydorus and Diomedes are fellow members of the Epigoni.
Polydorus is Hecuba's youngest son in Euripides.
Hecuba recognizes his murdered body and resolves to avenge him.

Polydorus.myth: Hecuba discovers Polydorus after Polyxena’s death
Polydorus.note: Their deaths jointly transform Hecuba’s grief into revenge, though they never converse.
Polydorus is Priam's son by Laothoe in Homer.
Polydorus is Semele’s brother in the Cadmean genealogy.

Polyeidus.note: The seer instructs Bellerophon to sleep beside Athena’s altar.

Polyidus.note: Minos imprisons or coerces Polyidus until the seer revives Glaucus.
Minos tries to compel Polyidus to teach divination to Glaucus.

Polymede.note: Apollodorus names Polymede, daughter of Autolycus, as Jason’s mother.

Polymedon.note: Polymedon is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Polymele.note: A variant attributed to Philocrates names Polymele as Patroclus’ mother.

Polymelus.note: Ixion kills Polymelus for murdering his mother after she rejected him.

Polymestor.note: Hecuba lures Polymestor into the women's tents with promises of hidden gold.
Hecuba kills his sons and blinds him for murdering Polydorus.
The blinded Polymestor foretells Hecuba's canine transformation and death at Cynossema.

Polyneices.note: Tiresias interprets the ritual pollution caused by Polyneices’s exposed corpse.

Polynices.note: Adrastus receives the exiled Polynices and promises to restore him.
Adrastus leads the Argive expedition on Polynices's behalf.
Amphiaraus condemns Polynices for attacking his own homeland.
Polynices bribes Eriphyle, indirectly forcing Amphiaraus into the doomed campaign.
Antigone hears his appeal and promises burial if circumstances permit.
Antigone performs dusting, libation, lament, and burial rites for him.
Antigone steals and secretly buries Polynices' body.
Antigone drags Polynices to Eteocles' burning pyre.
Antigone and Argia place Polynices upon Eteocles' pyre.
Antigone and Argia find and burn Polynices' body together.
Antigone carries him toward Eteocles' tomb to reconcile the brothers.
Cadmus is Polynices’s ancestor through the Labdacid royal line.
Polynices is one of Oedipus’s two securely established sons.
Oedipus refuses Polynices’s request and curses the brothers to mutual death.

Polyphemus the Lapith.note: Nestor recalls the Lapith Polyphemus as his comrade against the Centaurs.

Polypoetes.note: Polypoetes is Odysseus' son by Callidice.

Polytechnus.note: In the Anatolian variant, Aëdon, Procne's analogue, marries Polytechnus.
Aëdon competes with Polytechnus after Eris provokes their craftsmanship contest.
Aëdon and Chelidon kill Itys and serve him to Polytechnus.
Polytechnus rapes Chelidon and disguises her as a slave in Aëdon's household.

Polyxenus.note: Hellanicus makes Polyxenus, rather than Medus, Medea's son by Jason.

Polyxo.note: Polyxo receives exiled Helen on Rhodes, then engineers her hanging.

Poseidon Hippios.note: A temple of Poseidon Hippios is attributed to Trophonius and Agamedes.

Procris.note: Minos desires Procris, who first cures the sexual affliction Pasiphae imposed on him.
Minos rewards Procris with magical hunting gifts after she cures his affliction.

Procrustes.note: Theseus kills Procrustes by applying his own bed-torture.

Proetus.note: Some late genealogies add Proetus as Palamedes’s brother.
A minority tradition makes Proetus Perseus’ mortal father.

Promachus.note: Promachus and Diomedes are fellow members of the Epigoni.

Pronax.note: Pronax is Adrastus's brother in Pseudo-Apollodorus's genealogy.

Pronoia.note: One textually uncertain Catalogue reading makes Pronoia Deucalion's mother.

Pronous.note: Hecataeus makes Pronous Deucalion's son and Hellen's father.

Prote.note: A Byzantine variant names Prote as Phaethon's mother.

Protogeneia.note: Protogeneia is the daughter of Deucalion and Pyrrha.

Psamathe.note: Psamathe sends a wolf against Peleus’ herds to avenge her son Phocus.
Aeacus sexually pursues Psamathe despite her transformation and fathers Phocus.

Pterelaus.note: Amphitryon attacks Pterelaus’ kingdom but cannot prevail while the king retains his golden hair.

Ptoliporthes.note: Later genealogy names Ptoliporthes as a son by Penelope.
Ptoliporthes is a further son of Penelope and Odysseus.

Pylades.note: The Nostoi pairs Pylades with Orestes in the vengeance culminating in Clytemnestra’s death.
Pylades invokes Apollo’s oracle, overcoming Orestes’ hesitation to kill Clytemnestra.
Castor or Apollo assigns Electra to marry Pylades; later mythographers repeat the marriage.
Pylades accompanies Orestes, and Electra crowns him during the revenge narrative.
Pylades joins Orestes in the attempted killing of Helen.

Pylades.myth: Letter recognition and escape from Tauris
Pylades.note: He accepts her letter, helps reveal her identity, and joins the escape.
Pylades is Orestes’ foster-brother and exemplary lifelong companion.
Pylades reminds the wavering Orestes of Apollo’s command.
Pylades accompanies Orestes to Tauris and helps him escape.
Pylades helps Orestes attack Helen and seize Hermione.

Pylaemenes.note: Menelaus kills Pylaemenes, although a later passage appears to show him alive.

Pylartes.note: Patroclus kills Pylartes during his final assault toward Troy.

Pyraechmes.myth: Patroclus drives Trojans from the ships
Pyraechmes.note: Patroclus kills the Paeonian leader Pyraechmes.

Pyrois.myth: Phaethon loses control of the solar horses
Pyrois.note: Pyrois bolts with the team when Phaethon cannot govern the chariot.

Rhadamanthys of Wyvern.note: Modern media reinvents Rhadamanthus as the armored Specter Rhadamanthys of Wyvern.

Rhesus.note: Diomedes kills Rhesus while he sleeps in the Thracian camp.
Diomedes and Odysseus seize Rhesus’ horses after killing him.
Hector receives the late Thracian ally and disputes his delayed arrival.
Odysseus helps raid Rhesus and removes his horses after Diomedes kills him.

Rhexenor.note: Rhexenor is one of Diomedes’ companions transformed into a bird.

Rhode.note: One scholastic genealogy makes Rhode, daughter of Asopus, Phaethon's mother.

Rhoecus.note: Atalanta fights Rhoecus when he attempts to rape her.
Atalanta shoots and kills the assaulting centaur Rhoecus.

Rhoeo.note: A later genealogical variant names Rhoeo as Jason’s mother.

Roman Hercules.note: Roman religion identifies Heracles with Hercules while adding Italic cult traditions.

Salmoneus.note: Sisyphus plots to father descendants who will kill his hated brother.

Sangarius.note: Apollodorus records the river-god Sangarius as Hecuba's father.
A later alternative makes the river-god Sangarius Paris's maternal grandfather.

Saon.note: Trophonius teaches Saon the oracle’s ritual after bees reveal the chasm.

Satyrs.note: Dramatic and visual traditions place hammering or dancing satyrs around Pandora.
Satyrs.source: Sophocles, Pandora or Hammerers; related pottery

Scamander.note: The river attacks Achilles for choking its waters with Trojan corpses.

Scamandrius.note: Scamandrius, called Astyanax by the Trojans, is Hector's only securely early son.

Scamandrius.myth: Helmet scene at the Scaean Gates
Scamandrius.note: Hector removes his frightening helmet, embraces his son and prays for his future strength.

Scarphe.note: A later genealogical variant names Scarphe as Jason’s mother.

Schedius.note: Hector kills Schedius during the Trojan War.

Schoeneus.note: Schoeneus is Atalanta’s father in the Boeotian genealogy.
He establishes or administers her footrace and marriage conditions.

Sciron.note: Sciron is Peleus’ maternal grandfather through Endeis in Apollodorus.
Sciron is Aeacus’s father-in-law in one genealogy of Endeis.
Theseus throws Sciron from the cliff where he murdered travellers.
A Megarian version makes Sciron a respectable relative or military leader.

Sesostris.myth: Competing identity of the vocal statue
Sesostris.note: Pausanias reports a competing claim that the statue represented Sesostris.

Seven sons and seven daughters.note: A scholastic regional tradition gives Medea fourteen children.
Corinthian women kill Medea's fourteen children for rejecting the foreign sorceress.

Silenus.note: Midas' men bind Silenus and present him before the enthroned king.
Midas captures the satyr by mixing wine into a spring.
An Ancyra tradition likewise says Midas captured Silenus using wine.
Silenus tells Midas that nonexistence, then early death, is humanity's greatest good.
Silenus describes immense outer continents and the cities Eusebes and Machimos.
Midas recognizes, entertains, and restores the lost Silenus to Dionysus.

Simoeisius.note: Ajax kills the young Trojan Simoeisius.

Sinis.note: Theseus kills Sinis by the same pine-torture used on travellers.

Solymi.note: Bellerophon fights and defeats the Solymi in his hardest battle.

Spartoi.note: Cadmus sows the dragon’s teeth, from which the armed Spartoi arise.
Cadmus throws a stone among them, provoking their mutual slaughter.

Spercheius.note: A variant credits the river-god Spercheius with biological paternity of Peleus’ putative daughter Polydora.

Spercheus.note: Achilles gives Patroclus the hair previously vowed to the river Spercheus.

Sterope.note: Sterope is falsely named to Antigone as the woman Peleus intends to marry.

Stheneboea.note: She propositions Bellerophon, who refuses her invitation to secret intercourse.
After rejection, she falsely claims Bellerophon attempted to violate her.
Bellerophon carries her on Pegasus and drops her into the sea.

Sthenelaus son of Ithaemenes.note: Patroclus kills Sthenelaus with a stone blow to the neck.

Sthenele.note: One Apollodoran genealogy names Sthenele as Patroclus’ mother.

Sthenelus.myth: Sthenelus expels the couple after Electryon’s death
Sthenelus.note: Sthenelus drives Amphitryon, Alcmene, and Licymnius into exile.
Sthenelus is a son of Andromeda and Perseus.
Sthenelus serves as Diomedes’ closest battlefield companion and charioteer.
Diomedes and Sthenelus participate together among the victorious Epigoni.
Sthenelus is listed among the sons of Perseus and Andromeda.

Stheno.note: Stheno pursues Perseus after he decapitates Medusa.

Stilbe.note: A scholion names Stilbe as Callisto’s mother.

Stratius.note: Stratius is one of Nestor’s sons present at Pylos.

Strophius.note: Strophius receives and fosters Orestes after the child is removed from Clytemnestra’s household.
Hellanicus, as cited by Pausanias, names Strophius as Electra’s son by Pylades.
Electra entrusts her rescued infant brother to the Phocian king Strophius.
The Phocian king shelters and raises the exiled Orestes.

Stymphalus.note: Pelops pretends friendship with the Arcadian king before attacking him.
Pelops kills, dismembers, and scatters Stymphalus’s body.
Aeacus ends the sterility attributed to the pollution from Stymphalus’s dismemberment.

Talaus.note: Talaus is Adrastus's father in the earliest secure genealogy.
Later tradition makes Amphiaraus the killer of Adrastus’ father Talaus.

Talthybius.note: Agamemnon's herald helps remove Briseis from Achilles.
Talthybius acts for Agamemnon in later traditions surrounding Iphigenia's sacrifice.
Talthybius announces the sentence and removes Astyanax from Andromache.
The herald helps fetch Iphigenia from Clytemnestra under the marriage pretext.
Talthybius restrains axe-bearing Clytemnestra as she rushes to defend Aegisthus.
Talthybius reports Polyxena's sacrifice to Hecuba.
Talthybius brings Hecuba Astyanax's body and reports his sentence.

Talthybius.myth: Fetching Iphigenia for the false wedding
Talthybius.note: He accompanies Odysseus to obtain her under the false marriage claim.
Talthybius communicates collective decisions associated with Odysseus in tragedy.
Talthybius announces the decision and recounts Polyxena’s courageous death to Hecuba.

Tantalus, son of Thyestes.note: Tantalus was Clytemnestra’s first husband before Agamemnon killed him.

Taurus.note: Taurus is Minos’s general or champion in rationalized traditions.

Taygete.note: Taygete is one variant mother of Niobe.

Tecmessa.note: Tecmessa is Ajax’s captive partner and mother of Eurysaces.
Tecmessa pleads against Ajax’s suicide, finds his body, and mourns.

Telamon.note: Telamon rebukes Jason for leaving Heracles, then reconciles and continues the voyage.
Telamon and Atalanta appear together among the Calydonian hunters.
Telamon assists Heracles in Troy’s sack and receives Hesione.
Telamon sharply criticizes Jason after Heracles is abandoned, then reconciles with him.
Telamon appears with Meleager among the assembled hunters.
Telamon and Meleager sail together as Argonauts.
Telamon is normally Peleus’ full brother.
Peleus and Telamon jointly plot against and conceal the killing of Phocus.
The Aeacid brothers participate together in the Argonautic expedition.
Aeacus expels Telamon and refuses him permission to land during his defense.

Telecleia.note: Later scholia variously name Telecleia as Hecuba's mother.

Teledamus.note: Later mythography makes Teledamus a twin son of Agamemnon and Cassandra.
Teledamus is Cassandra’s infant son by Agamemnon.
A later genealogy makes Teledamus his son by Calypso.

Telegonus.note: Telegonus is Odysseus' son by Circe.
Telegonus unknowingly kills Odysseus with a stingray-tipped spear.
A conflicting genealogy makes Telegonus his son by Calypso.
Telegonus carries Penelope to Circe after accidentally killing Odysseus.
Penelope becomes Telegonus’s wife after Odysseus’s death.
Telegonus is Telemachus’ paternal half-brother, born to Odysseus and Circe.

Telegonus.myth: Journey to Circe after Odysseus’ death
Telegonus.note: Telegonus transports Telemachus, Penelope, and Odysseus’ body to Circe.

Telephassa.note: Telephassa, also called Argiope, is Cadmus’s mother.
Telephassa accompanies Cadmus’s search and dies in Thrace.

Telephus.note: Achilles wounds Telephus during the Greeks’ mistaken expedition to Mysia.
Achilles heals Telephus, who afterward guides the Greeks toward Troy.
Agamemnon's forces fight Telephus after mistakenly landing in Mysia.
After healing, Telephus guides Agamemnon's expedition toward Troy.
Dramatic variants bring Telephus as a suppliant into Agamemnon's household.
On Clytemnestra’s advice, Telephus seizes infant Orestes to obtain a cure.
Telephus is Heracles’ son by Auge.
Telephus seizes infant Orestes to compel healing and guidance to Troy.
Patroclus supports Achilles when Telephus routs the Achaeans in Mysia.

Telestas.note: Telestas is listed among Priam's sons by other women.

Tenes.note: Achilles kills Tenes despite Thetis’ warning, provoking Apollo’s eventual vengeance.

Tereus.note: Procne is given to Tereus in marriage after his alliance with Pandion.

Tereus.myth: Tereus separates and conceals the sisters
Tereus.note: Tereus deceives both sisters, concealing his violence against Philomela from Procne.
Tereus rapes Philomela, cuts out her tongue, and confines her.
The sisters serve Tereus his murdered son and reveal the deception.
Tereus pursues the fleeing sisters with a weapon before their transformations.

Teucer.note: Teucer is Ajax’s half-brother through Telamon.
Teucer shoots from behind Ajax’s great shield.
Teucer defends Ajax’s burial and becomes Eurysaces’ guardian.
Teucer repeatedly shoots at Hector, who eventually wounds him with a stone.
Teucer opposes Menelaus’ order forbidding burial of Ajax.
Aeacus is Teucer’s grandfather through Telamon.
Teucer resists Sarpedon's Lycian assault, wounding Glaucus rather than Sarpedon.

Teumessian fox.myth: Amphitryon counters the uncatchable Teumessian fox
Teumessian fox.note: Amphitryon must resolve the fox’s depredations before Creon will support his war.

Teuthras.note: Hector kills Teuthras during the Trojan War.

Thamyris.note: Thamyris and Orpheus are paired as primordial Thracian singers.
Through Menippe, one late genealogy makes Orpheus the grandson of Thamyris.

Thasus.note: Cadmus’s kinsman or companion leaves the search and settles Thasos.

The Argive mothers.myth: Supplication and recovery of the dead
The Argive mothers.note: Adrastus and the mothers jointly supplicate at Eleusis and recover their sons' bodies.

The Epigoni.note: Adrastus accompanies or leads the Epigoni in their successful conquest of Thebes.
Tiresias foresees defeat and becomes captive or dedicated spoil after Thebes falls.

The Fates.note: The Fates join Poseidon in exacting posthumous vengeance for Palamedes.

The Ismenian dragon.note: Cadmus battles the dragon after it kills his water-fetching companions.
Cadmus kills the dragon and subsequently sows its teeth.

The Moirai.note: At his birth they bind Meleager's lifespan to a burning billet.

The Olympian gods.note: The gods bury Niobe's children on the tenth day.
The sisters pray for escape and are transformed into a nightingale and swallow.

The Peliades.note: Medea tricks them with a ram demonstration into cutting up Pelias.

The Plataean founder heroes.myth: Sacrifices before the battle of Plataea
The Plataean founder heroes.note: Actaeon is grouped with local founder heroes whom the Greeks must honor.

The Propoetides.note: Their punished conduct leads Pygmalion to reject relations with women and remain unmarried.

The Sipylian nymphs.note: Petrified Niobe remains near the Sipylian nymphs' dancing grounds; they do not address her.

The gods.note: The gods grant Protesilaus a temporary return in response to Laodamia's request.

Theano.note: One variant says Theano hands the Palladium to Diomedes and Odysseus.
Later genealogists make Hecuba and Theano sisters through Cisseus.
Hecuba gives Theano a robe to place upon Athena's knees.
Theano cites Penthesilea's trained prowess while dissuading Trojan women from fighting.

Theoclymenus.note: Theoclymenus attempts to compel Helen to marry him.
Helen deceives Theoclymenus with a false funeral and escapes Egypt.
Menelaus and Helen deceive Theoclymenus to secure their escape from Egypt.
Telemachus accepts the fugitive seer aboard his ship and brings him to Ithaca.
The seer interprets favorable omens concerning Telemachus’ family.

Theognete.note: A later genealogical variant names Theognete as Jason’s mother.

Theonoe.note: Theonoe conceals Menelaus’s presence and assists Helen’s escape.
Theonoe conceals Menelaus’ presence and enables his escape with Helen.

Thermodosa.note: Thermodosa accompanies Penthesilea and is killed by Meriones.

Thersander.note: Adrastus is Thersander's grandfather through Argia and Polynices.
Adrastus accompanies Thersander and the other Epigoni against Thebes.
Thersander and Diomedes are fellow members of the Epigoni.
Thersander is named as a son of Sisyphus.

Thersites.note: Achilles kills Thersites for mocking his alleged love for dead Penthesilea.
Thersites publicly denounces Agamemnon's greed before Odysseus silences him.
Polygnotus depicts Ajax playing dice with Thersites as Odysseus’s enemies.
Odysseus publicly rebukes and strikes Thersites.
Palamedes and Thersites play dice in Polygnotus’s Delphi painting.
Thersites gouges or strikes the dead Penthesilea's eye with his spear.
Thersites mocks Achilles over his alleged love for Penthesilea.

Thestius.note: Thestius is Amphiaraus’ maternal grandfather in later genealogies.
The dominant post-Homeric genealogy makes Leda a daughter of Thestius.

Thestor son of Enops.note: Patroclus kills Thestor at close quarters inside his chariot.

Thoas.note: She persuades Thoas that the captives and image require seaside purification.
Thoas pursues the escaping Iphigenia until Athena orders him to desist.
Some later sources make Thoas a son of Jason and Hypsipyle.
Thoas appears among opponents attributed to Menelaus’ battlefield kill list.
Orestes participates in Iphigenia’s deception of the pursuing Taurian king.

Thrasius.note: A possibly distinct Pygmalion is father of the seer Thrasius.

Thrasymedes.note: Thrasymedes is Nestor’s son and a warrior at Troy.
Thrasymedes assists his father’s household in Athena’s sacrifice.

Thrasymelus.note: Patroclus kills Sarpedon’s companion immediately before attacking Sarpedon.
Thrasymelus accompanies Sarpedon in his final engagement and is killed by Patroclus.

Thyestes.note: Agamemnon's uncle is a dynastic rival whose murdered children motivate Aegisthus' vengeance.
Thyestes is a recurrent son of Pelops and Hippodamia.
Pelops curses and exiles Thyestes for involvement in Chrysippus’s murder.
Thyestes is Tantalus’s grandson through Pelops.

Thyestes.myth: Atreus repeats the ancestral cannibal feast
Thyestes.note: Thyestes suffers the feast that repeats Tantalus’s crime under his ghost’s influence.

Thyia.note: Thyia is named as Deucalion's daughter.

Thymbraeus.note: Hyginus names Thymbraeus as one of Laocoön’s sons.
Laocoön attempts unsuccessfully to save Thymbraeus during the serpent attack.

Timandra.note: Timandra is Clytemnestra’s sister in the Hesiodic genealogy.
Their abandonment or dishonouring of husbands is paired in archaic genealogy.
Timandra is the daughter of Leda and Tyndareus.

Timothea.note: Timothea is Midas' wife and Anchurus' mother in the chasm narrative.

Tiphys.note: Tiphys serves as Argo’s original helmsman until dying from illness.

Tisamenus.note: In an inconsistent later genealogy, Tisamenus is assigned to Jason and Medea.
Tisamenus is Orestes’ son and successor by Hermione.

Tisiphone.note: Penthesilea's example inspires Tisiphone to urge Trojan women into battle.
Rhadamanthus sends convicted souls to Tisiphone for punishment.
One inconsistent genealogy makes Tisiphone Tiresias’s descendant through Manto.

Tithonus.note: Tithonus is Memnon’s mortal Trojan father.
Later genealogical systematization lists Tithonus among Priam's siblings.

Tityos.note: Ixion and Tityos are jointly listed among the great infernal offenders.
Tityos is placed near Tantalus among exemplary underworld sufferers.

Tityus.note: Rhadamanthus travels to Euboea to see Tityus for an unstated purpose.

Tlepolemus.note: Philoctetes aids Rhodian settlers associated with Tlepolemus, not necessarily Tlepolemus personally.
They exchange challenges and simultaneously cast spears, with Sarpedon wounded in the thigh.
Sarpedon's spear strikes Tlepolemus through the neck and kills him.

Tmolus.note: Hyginus' compressed genealogy possibly makes Tmolus Midas' father.
Tmolus awards Apollo victory, but Midas challenges his verdict.
Tmolus replaces Zeus as Tantalus’s father in a minority genealogy.

Toxeus.note: Toxeus joins in denying Atalanta the trophy and taking it from her.
Meleager kills his maternal uncle Toxeus during the trophy dispute.

Trechus.note: Hector kills Trechus during the Trojan War.

Triptolemus.note: Rhadamanthus and Triptolemus appear together among Socrates’s true judges.
Aeacus and Triptolemus appear together among Socrates’s true judges.

Troezen.note: Troezen is Pelops’s son or descendant and the city’s eponym.

Troilos.note: Achilles ambushes, pursues, and kills Troilos, often at Apollo’s altar.

Troilus.note: Troilus is included among Cassandra’s Trojan brothers.
Apollodorus lists Troilus as Hecuba's son, fathered by Priam or Apollo.

Troilus.myth: Achilles ambushes Troilus and Polyxena at the fountain
Troilus.note: Polyxena escapes while Achilles pursues her brother Troilus.
Priam regards Troilus as his son, though some traditions name Apollo as father.

Tros.note: Tros belongs to Hector's direct Trojan royal ancestry.
Paris belongs to the royal line descended from Tros.
Tros is Priam's dynastic ancestor and namesake of the Trojans.

Tydeus.note: Adrastus receives Tydeus, marries Deipyle to him, and promises restoration.
Adrastus makes Tydeus a champion in the war against Thebes.
Amphiaraus condemns his fellow commander Tydeus as murderous.
Amphiaraus induces Tydeus to eat a brain, costing him Athena’s immortality.
Tydeus allegedly kills Antigone and Ismene in an early variant.
Tydeus is Diomedes’ father and the heroic standard used to judge him.

Tyndareus.note: Later tradition makes Tyndareus protector of the exiled Agamemnon and Menelaus.
Tyndareus helps restore Agamemnon and becomes his father-in-law.
Dominant genealogy names Tyndareus as Clytemnestra’s mortal father.
Tyndareus supports the prosecution and punishment of Electra and Orestes for matricide.
Tyndareus is Helen’s reputed human father or foster-father.
Tyndareus exacts the suitors’ oath and arranges Helen’s marriage.
He is her maternal grandfather in the standard genealogy.
Leda is Tyndareus’s wife and queen of his Spartan household.
Tyndareus gives or permits Helen in marriage to Menelaus.
Orestes is Tyndareus’ maternal grandson through Clytemnestra.
Tyndareus denounces the matricide and presses politically for Orestes’ punishment.
Tyndareus helps Odysseus obtain Penelope after receiving his advice.

Tyro.note: Tyro and Narcissus are jointly listed among the beautiful dead.
Sisyphus impregnates his niece Tyro to produce avengers against Salmoneus.

Tyro’s two sons.note: Sisyphus fathers two unnamed sons by Tyro.

Udaeus.note: Udaeus survives the Spartoi conflict and becomes a Theban ancestor.
Later mythography places Tiresias in Udaeus’s Spartoi lineage.

Ulisse.note: Ulisse is Dante's medieval Italian form and reinvention of Odysseus.

Unnamed twin sister.note: Narcissus has an identical twin sister in Pausanias' rationalization.
Narcissus loves her and uses his reflection as consolation after her death.

Uthuze.note: Etruscan Uthuze is the visual-cultural adaptation of Greek Odysseus.

Virbius.note: Greek and Roman writers identify the revived hero with Aricia’s divine Virbius.

Virbius the younger.note: Virgil anomalously makes the resurrected Hippolytus father of a younger Virbius.

Xanthias.note: Aeacus subjects Xanthias and Dionysus to comic interrogation and whipping.

Xanthus.note: A rationalized account replaces Zeus with Xanthus as Sarpedon's father.

Xanthus and Balius.note: The immortal horses draw Achilles’ chariot; Xanthus prophesies his death.

Xenodice.note: Xenodice is listed among Minos’s children by Pasiphae.

Zetes.note: Zetes serves in the company and pursues the Harpies from Phineus.
Zetes accompanies Jason and helps drive the Harpies away from Phineus.
Zetes and Orpheus serve together among the Argonauts.

Zethus.note: Zethus is Amphion's brother and therefore Niobe's brother-in-law.
An alternative tradition makes Zethus Niobe's husband.
In the Homeric parallel, Aëdon, the analogue of Procne, is Zethus's wife.

Zeus Basileus.note: Consultants sacrifice to Zeus Basileus before entering Trophonius’ oracle.

Zeus Idaios.note: An altar of Zeus Idaios is founded after Midas' son sacrifices himself.

Zeus Kappotas.note: Orestes’ madness ends when he sits upon the god’s sacred stone.

Zeus’ mountain nymphs.note: The nymphs plant elms around the burial mound of Andromache’s father.

Zeuxippe.note: Zeuxippe is the mother of Philomela and Procne.

Zoe.note: Popular internet retellings invent Zoe as Midas' daughter without ancient support.

daughter of Thoas.note: An Aetolian tradition has Odysseus marry Thoas' unnamed daughter.

sons of Asclepius.note: Heracles promises that the sons of Asclepius will cure Philoctetes.

the Centaurs.note: Nestor fought beside Lapith heroes against the mountain-dwelling Centaurs.

the Danaids.note: The Danaids’ infernal punishment temporarily ceases while Orpheus sings.
Later art and literature group the Danaids with Tantalus in Hades.

the Delphians.note: Delphians stone and attack Neoptolemus before one delivers the fatal blow.
The dead Neoptolemus aids Delphi against the Galatian attack.

the Fates.note: Later accounts assign Pelops’s restoration to the Fates collectively.

the Phineids.note: Their mutilation and confinement parallel Antigone's familial suffering.

the gods.note: The gods admire Alcestis’ courage and return her soul from death.
Camus recasts Sisyphus as consciously defying the gods' intended humiliation.

the suitors.note: Penelope delays the suitors for three years by unweaving Laertes’s shroud nightly.
Penelope challenges the suitors to string Odysseus’s bow and shoot through twelve axes.
Penelope induces the suitors to present clothing and jewelry as courtship gifts.
Duris makes all the suitors collectively father Pan with Penelope.

the two serpents.myth: Serpent omen at the Wooden Horse
the two serpents.note: Two serpents kill Laocoön and one son; his other son survives.
Laocoön struggles to rescue his sons before the serpents bind and kill him.
The serpents seize both sons, bind Laocoön, and kill him.
Laocoön survives blinded while the serpents summoned by Athena kill his sons.

the unnamed infant by Tantalus.note: Clytemnestra’s unnamed infant by Tantalus was killed by Agamemnon.

unnamed daughter of Ocean.note: A competing genealogy makes an unnamed Oceanid Helen’s mother.

unnamed ivory woman.note: Pygmalion carves her from ivory before Venus brings her to life.

unnamed ivory woman.myth: Marriage of Pygmalion and the animated woman
unnamed ivory woman.note: Pygmalion embraces and marries the animated woman, who later bears Paphos.
